sentence: The sleeper out of Hanoi rocked us north through a darkness that smelled of coal smoke and wet rice. I lay in the upper berth tracing the rattle of couplings, listening to a woman two compartments down sing softly to a child who would not settle. By the time grey light leaked under the blind, the carriage had filled with the green steam of terraced hills, and the conductor came through with tin cups of tea so strong it tasted of the engine.

Somewhere past midnight the train stopped in a station with no name I could read, and through the fogged glass I watched a man sell hard-boiled eggs from a bicycle basket to passengers leaning down from open windows. The platform lamps swung in a wind off the steppe. I bought two eggs and a fistful of sunflower seeds, paid in coins I could not count, and the train pulled away before I had finished thanking him.

On the Caledonian sleeper the steward had warned me the dawn would be worth waking for, and it was. Rannoch Moor unrolled outside the window in a sheet of bog cotton and standing water, the sky the colour of a pewter spoon. I drank my coffee standing in the corridor, the carriage swaying like a slow boat, and thought how rare it is now to arrive somewhere having watched the whole country slide beneath you.

The Indian Pacific takes three nights to cross the Nullarbor, and on the second the train simply stops in the dark so the passengers can step down onto the sand and look up. There is nothing out here, no town for five hundred miles, and the silence has a physical weight. The Milky Way hung overhead like spilled flour. A man beside me, who had not spoken all day, said quietly that he had waited forty years to see this.

We boarded the night train at Chiang Mai with a fan turning overhead and a vendor pushing a trolley of mango and sticky rice down the aisle. The berths folded down crisp and white, and I fell asleep to the jungle scrolling past, fireflies pricking the dark. I woke once at a junction to hear frogs roaring in a flooded paddy, then the long sigh of the brakes releasing, and we were moving again toward Bangkok.

The Trans-Mongolian crossed the border at Naushki in the small hours, and for three sleepless stops uniformed officers carried our passports away and brought them back stamped with cities I would never visit. Between inspections the train was lifted bodily so the bogies could be changed for the Russian gauge. I sat in the dark feeling the carriage rise on its jacks, and understood for the first time that a country can have a different idea of how wide a road should be.

There is a particular loneliness to the dining car of a night train, all white cloth and trembling cutlery, one waiter and three passengers who will never meet again. I ate beef stroganoff somewhere east of the Urals while a forest of birches went silver past the window. The waiter refilled my glass without asking and stood looking out with me, and neither of us said anything, because there was nothing to say that the country was not already saying.

On the overnight from Cairo the desert came right up to the rails, and at every halt the windows filled with the faces of boys selling bread and bottled water and dates pressed into bricks. I slept badly, the way one always does, and woke to the green shock of the Nile delta, canals threading between fields, white egrets standing in the wet like punctuation. The man across from me was already dressed and watching, as if he had never gone to sleep at all.

The Ghan rolled south out of Darwin into a dusk the colour of a struck match, and the dining car served barramundi while termite mounds went past like a city of small red chimneys. I had taken the train precisely because the plane was faster; there is a kind of travel that wants to be slow, that wants the distance to be felt in the body. By Alice Springs my watch meant nothing and the land had begun to mean everything.

We crossed into Switzerland while I was asleep, and the change announced itself before I opened my eyes: the rails ran quieter, the rhythm tightened, the train took the curves as if it had been wound by a watchmaker. When I lifted the blind the lake was there, perfectly still, holding the mountains upside down, and a man in a rowing boat was already out on it, gathering whatever it is the early water gives.

In the last village before the pass an old woman waved me in from the rain without a word, and within minutes I was sitting by a stove with a bowl of barley soup and three generations watching me eat it. They spoke no language I knew, and I none of theirs, but the grandfather kept refilling my cup of buttermilk and the children laughed every time I burned my mouth, and I have rarely felt so completely a guest.

The trail ended at a stone house where a shepherd was making cheese, and he set down his work to walk me to the spring, fill my bottle, and refuse the coins I held out as if I had offered him an insult. He gave me instead a wedge of that morning's cheese wrapped in a dock leaf, pointed at the ridge I had to climb, and went back inside. I ate it on the col, looking down at his roof, the only roof for miles.

Snow had closed the road, so the bus simply stopped in a village of perhaps forty people, and a family took six stranded passengers into their kitchen for the night. We slept on quilts by the fire, and in the morning the mother had baked bread for all of us and would hear nothing of payment. The father walked us to where the plough had cut through, and stood waving until the bend in the road took him.

High in the Atlas a man invited me for tea that turned into three glasses, then a meal, then a bed, the hospitality unfolding with the slow inevitability of something that could not be refused without giving offence. His wife served us and did not eat with us; his sons asked me about my country with a curiosity so genuine it shamed my own. In the morning he pressed walnuts into my pack and said the mountain would look after me, as it had looked after them.

I had not asked for shelter, only for directions, but the woman at the well looked at the sky, looked at my thin jacket, and that was the end of my plans for the day. Her house smelled of woodsmoke and drying herbs, and her husband came in from the terraces at dusk smelling of the same. They fed me potatoes and a hard salty cheese and asked nothing of me, and I lay awake a long time wondering what I had done to deserve it, and concluded: nothing, which is the whole point.

The teahouse in the Khumbu was really just a family's front room with a stove and a row of foam mattresses, and the daughter who served the dal bhat could not have been twelve. She moved between the trekkers and her homework with the same competence, and when the power failed she lit butter lamps and kept ladling rice. Outside, Ama Dablam caught the last light. Inside, a child was carrying a whole valley's economy on a tin tray, and smiling about it.

An avalanche had taken the path, and so I spent two extra days in a village that received me like weather: something that had arrived and would, in time, move on. The headman gave me his son's room. The women taught me to card wool, badly. A boy walked me each morning to the edge of the snow to see if it had melted, and each morning it had not, and each evening we walked back, and he seemed entirely content with this arrangement, as in the end was I.

In a hamlet below the glacier a man mending a fence put down his hammer to brew me coffee in a pot black with use, and we drank it on an upturned crate watching his goats work the slope. He had been to the city once, he said, and had not cared for it. The mountains gave him everything: the water, the cheese, the quiet, and now, he said with a grin, an unexpected foreigner to practise his three English words on.

The bus to the valley head left only when it was full, and the village waited for it together, so that by the time we boarded I had been given an apple, a seat, and the life story of the woman beside me, translated by a teenager keen to practise. When my stop came the whole bus seemed to know it before I did, and a chorus of voices made sure I did not miss it, and I stepped down feeling I had been delivered rather than merely transported.

I knocked at a farmhouse to ask if the spring water was safe, and left an hour later having drunk the water, eaten the lunch, admired the new calf, and promised to send a photograph I would in fact send. The old farmer walked me to his gate and pointed across the valley to where his own father was buried, on a knoll among pines, and said that he had never wished to be anywhere else, and that he hoped, wherever I was going, I would one day feel the same about somewhere.

The frontier between the two countries was a striped pole, a tin shed, and a soldier so young he was still growing into his uniform. I handed over my passport and watched him work through it page by page, sounding out the stamps like a boy reading aloud. Behind him the same hills rolled on, indifferent to the line we had all agreed to draw across them, and a goat wandered through no-man's-land cropping the grass of two nations at once.

You walk the last hundred metres of one country and the first hundred of the next, and in between there is a strip of nowhere where the road is unswept and the flags hang on separate poles. I crossed at dawn with a line of traders pushing bicycles loaded with sacks, and the only sound was the squeak of wheels and the thump of stamps. On the far side a different alphabet announced itself on the first shop sign, and the journey, which had felt continuous, suddenly had a seam.

The border post sat at four thousand metres and the wind came through the pass like a punishment. I queued in it for an hour with porters and pilgrims, breath smoking, while officials in two languages decided I was harmless. When at last the barrier lifted I walked into the new country light-headed from altitude and relief, and the prayer flags strung across the road snapped and streamed as if applauding everyone who made it through.

On the bridge between the two towns the planks were worn to a shine by a century of feet, and halfway across, the river beneath me belonged to neither side or to both. A woman ahead of me carried a live chicken under each arm; a man behind me carried a television. We were all simply going to market, and the line on the map meant only that we would pay our duties and be searched, and then go on being the same people we had been on the other bank.

I had imagined the desert frontier as something dramatic, and instead it was a man at a card table under a tarpaulin, a thermos beside him, and a dog asleep in the only shade for kilometres. He stamped me out of one nation, walked me twenty metres to a colleague who stamped me into the next, and the two of them shared the thermos and clearly shared their lunches too. The desert did not recognise the distinction, and after an hour's walking, neither did I.

Crossing on foot you learn things the car traveller never does: the exact width of the buffer zone, the smell of the duty-free coffee the guards drink, the way the asphalt changes texture at the precise point sovereignty changes hands. I walked through with a Belgian cyclist and a family of returning migrants, and we three parties, who had nothing in common, became briefly a small society united by the shared and faintly absurd ritual of being permitted to continue.

The river was the border and the ferry was a man with a pole, and he took me across at the price of a conversation about the rains. On the far bank the customs house had no glass in its windows and a typewriter on the desk, and the officer carbon-copied my details into a ledger that went back, by the look of it, decades. I thought of all the names in that book, everyone who had ever stood where I stood, wanting only to be on the other side.

Walking out of the mountains I reached the frontier at dusk, when both posts were closing, and was waved through with a haste that suggested everyone wanted their dinner. The new country began with a hand-painted sign and a different brand of cigarette in the kiosk window. I changed my last coins for the local currency with a man who did the sum on his fingers, and walked on into a town whose lights were just coming up, a stranger again, which is its own kind of freedom.

The crossing was high in a green saddle between two ranges, and a cow had lain down across the painted line so that the truck behind me had to wait while a guard, laughing, persuaded it to move. The animal did not understand borders and the guard did not really seem to either. He stamped my book, scratched the cow's ear, and pointed me down the far slope into a valley where, he promised, the cheese was better.

I crossed from one country into another along a path through a beech wood, the only marker a granite stone half-swallowed by moss and carved with the date some surveyor had decided this was the edge of things. No guard, no gate, just the wood continuing and a buzzard turning overhead in airspace it had never been told was divided. I sat on the stone and ate an apple and was, for those few minutes, a citizen of neither and of the wood itself.

The fish market opened before the sun, lit by bare bulbs strung between posts, and the floor ran with melted ice and silver scales. Men in rubber boots heaved tuna onto trestles, and the auctioneer's chant rose and fell like a tide. I stood out of the way with a paper cup of coffee, watching a city feed itself in the dark, and by the time the sky paled the best of the catch was already gone, sold, boxed, and rattling away on the backs of mopeds.

At first light the flower sellers were already at their stalls, and the whole square smelled of cut stems and wet newspaper. An old woman bound marigolds into garlands with a speed her fingers seemed to manage without her, gossiping the while with the woman beside her. The marigolds were for the temple, she told me, for the gods, who like the rest of us preferred their flowers fresh, and best of all at the cool clean start of the day.

The market set up in darkness, each trader unrolling a tarp and arranging a small kingdom of produce by torchlight. By the time the muezzin called, the aisles were a river of bodies, and the spice merchant beside me had built pyramids of turmeric and paprika so precise they looked carved. I bought a paper twist of saffron and a handful of dates, and ate the dates walking, the sun finally clearing the rooftops and pouring gold down the lanes.

Dawn at the floating market is a slow collision of boats, each piled with pomelos or chillies or coconuts, the women paddling them standing up with a single oar. Trade happens hull to hull, money and fruit passed across the gap. I drank a coffee handed up from a boat with a charcoal stove in it, sweetened thick with condensed milk, and watched the canal fill with colour as the light came on like something switched.

The livestock market began in the cold before dawn, the breath of a thousand animals hanging over the pens like a low cloud. Farmers in felt hats stood in knots, talking prices, slapping flanks, sealing deals with a spit and a handshake. A boy led a reluctant calf in circles to show its paces. The whole scene had the unhurried certainty of something done this way for a very long time, and the sunrise, when it came, seemed almost an afterthought.

I reached the bread market while the ovens were still the loudest thing in the street, and the bakers were sliding flat loaves out on long peels and stacking them in towers that steamed in the cold. People queued in dressing gowns and slippers, half-asleep, holding cloths to carry the bread home in. The smell got into everything. I bought two rounds, ate one immediately, and understood that I had been invited, without knowing it, into the city's first secret of the day.

The morning market clung to a hillside, the stalls stepping down it in terraces so that you shopped by descending. At the top, herbs and bundled greens; lower down, the butchers; at the bottom, where the lane met the road, the women selling eggs from baskets lined with straw. I went down through it as the sun came over the ridge, and the light moved down the steps just ahead of me, as if it too were doing the morning's shopping.

Before six the spice souk was a tunnel of shuttered shops and one open stall, where a man was weighing cardamom into brass scales for a restaurant cook. The air was so dense with cinnamon and clove and dried lime that it seemed a thing you could lean on. He gave me a green cardamom pod to crack between my teeth, the taste flooding sharp and cool, and told me to come back at noon, when the place would be a different country entirely.

The Saturday market in the small town set up under plane trees still dripping from the night's rain, and the first customers were old men who came not to buy but to inspect, to weigh a melon in the hand and put it back, to greet every stallholder by name. By the time the families arrived the old men had finished their rounds and migrated to the café, and the market had warmed and loosened into the cheerful chaos it would keep until noon.

At dawn the vegetable wholesalers worked under the high tin roof in a din of trolleys and shouting, and a single shaft of sun came through a broken pane and lit the dust like a held breath. I had come for breakfast and found it at a stall in the corner: a bowl of noodles in broth, eaten standing, elbow to elbow with porters who had been awake for hours and would be awake for many more, the whole day's commerce already old news to them.

The last bus had gone and the next was at six, so I made a bed of my pack in the corner of the station where the heating pipes ran, and watched the night staff mop the floor in long slow arcs. A man who slept there every night, by the look of his arrangements, nodded to me as one nods to a colleague. I slept in snatches, woke to pigeons and the rattle of the first shutter, and stepped out into a morning that felt earned.

We pitched the tent in the dark by feel and headlamp, in a hollow we hoped was out of the wind and not in a watercourse, and lay listening to the canvas argue with the weather. At some point the rain started, found the seam it always finds, and dripped with great patience onto my left foot. I have slept in good hotels and remember none of them; I remember that hollow, that drip, the relief of the grey dawn, with a vividness that is almost love.

The bothy was a roofless ruin with one corner still sound, and I spread my bag in it and built a small fire of driftwood in the hearth that had not held one in years. The walls kept the wind off and the stars did the rest. I have a photograph of that night somewhere but I do not need it; the memory of lying there, warm in the cold, watching the smoke find the gap in the gable, is filed somewhere deeper than photographs reach.

Stranded by a missed connection, I slept in the bus on the verge of a desert road, the driver snoring across the front seats, the engine ticking as it cooled. The windows fogged with our breath. Outside, the dark was absolute and the silence had texture. I woke before everyone, wiped a porthole in the glass, and watched the horizon turn from black to a bruised, beautiful violet, the only witness to a sunrise the schedule had never intended me to see.

The hut on the ridge was first-come and already full, so I unrolled my mat on the porch with two other latecomers, and we lay in a row under the eaves like coins in a slot. The cold came up through the boards. Above us the sky was an outrageous spill of stars, and one of the strangers, a Czech woman, named the constellations softly in her own language until the third of us was asleep, and then, I think, until I was too.

I had not meant to spend the night on the beach, but the tide and the dark and a certain pleasant tiredness conspired, and I dug a hollow in the warm sand above the line of weed and lay down in it. The sea kept up its long argument with the shore. A dog appeared from somewhere, considered me, and curled against my back, and we kept each other warm until the fishermen came down at first light to drag their boats to the water.

When the storm closed the pass we sheltered under an overhang of rock, six strangers and a dog, building a fire of whatever the slope offered and feeding it carefully through the worst hours. We did not talk much. The fire was the conversation. By morning the snow had stopped and the world was blinding white and silent, and we put out the fire together, scattering the ash, and went our six ways as if the night had been a thing we had only imagined.

The night ferry was sold out of cabins, so I claimed a bench on the open deck and lay watching the funnel smoke unspool against the stars. Other deck sleepers had staked their own benches, wrapped in coats and unlikely blankets, a whole encampment of the thrifty and the late. The sea was kind. I slept and woke and slept, and each waking the coast was nearer, until the last one delivered me a harbour and the smell of land.

I spent a night in a half-built house on the edge of a town that was itself half-built, the concrete still smelling of its own newness, the window holes open to the dark. A watchman let me in for the price of sharing my bread. We sat on upturned buckets and he told me what each room would one day be, gesturing into the dark at the kitchen, the children's room, the future, and in the morning I left him to guard it all.

The shrine at the roadside had a roof and a wall and a stone shelf wide enough to lie on, and a traveller learns to recognise such gifts. I shared it that night with a pilgrim who had walked further than I had and complained less, and we lit a candle at the little altar, more for the light than the faith, and slept under the painted eyes of a saint who had presumably seen stranger guests than us.

I met him in the queue for the only working ATM in town, a Argentine who had been on the road for two years and spoke of it without a trace of boastfulness, as a man might speak of a job he happened to have. We ate together that night, and again the next, and then his bus came and mine did not, and that was that. I never learned his surname. I think of him more often than I think of people I have known for decades.

The hostel common room at midnight was a small United Nations: a Korean cook trading recipes with an Italian, a Dutchman mending a Brazilian's rucksack, two Australians arguing happily about a border crossing neither could pronounce. I had come down for water and stayed three hours. There is a particular friendship that forms among people who will never see each other again, frank and fast and weightless, and that room was full of it.

On the long bus a German girl shared her headphones with me, one ear each, and we watched the same desert go past to the same music for four hundred kilometres. We barely spoke. When she got off at her town she squeezed my arm and was gone into a crowd, and the song that had been playing finished without her, and I have never been able to hear it since without the window filling with that particular sand.

He was an old Englishman travelling alone, and he attached himself to our table at dinner with the practised ease of a man who had been doing this for fifty years. He had stories, of course, but the good thing about him was that he also wanted ours, and asked real questions, and remembered the answers. When he left he shook each of our hands and wished us, with great seriousness, good roads, and I have wished it of people ever since.

I shared a taxi from the airport with a stranger to split the fare, and by the time we reached the city we had agreed to climb the same volcano, and by the end of that climb we were the kind of friends that an ordinary year of ordinary life rarely produces. The mountain did it. Shared difficulty does it. We send each other photographs still, from our separate hemispheres, every time either of us stands somewhere high.

There was a Japanese man cycling the length of the continent, and we crossed paths three times in three countries, purely by chance, the way ships are said to. The first time we were strangers, the second acquaintances, the third old friends, the gaps between filled in by the simple fact of the road carrying us both the same way. The fourth crossing never came. I still scan the cyclists on every long road, half-hoping.

The Quebecois couple in the next tent had been everywhere and bored no one with it, and they cooked too much dinner on purpose so that the rest of the campsite would drift over. By the fire that night a Pole sang, a Kenyan translated a joke that lost nothing in the journey, and a small child belonging to nobody and everybody fell asleep in a circle of strangers who had become, for one evening, something very like a family.

I helped a woman carry her bag up the gangway and we ended up leaning on the same rail for the whole crossing, watching one island recede and another arrive. She was going home after twenty years away and was frightened of it, and said so, to me, a stranger, because a stranger was exactly the right person to say it to. When we docked she thanked me for the bag. I think she meant the listening.

The dormitory had eight beds and eight nationalities, and the unspoken treaty among us governed the light, the snoring, the small hours' return of the late. We were not friends and did not pretend to be, but there was a courtesy in that room, a recognition that we were all far from home and all, therefore, owed something. In the morning we nodded and scattered, and the treaty dissolved, having served.

A French cyclist with a broken spoke and no spares fell in with our group at a teahouse, and we adopted him for three days while a part was sought and found. He repaid us in stories and in a recklessness with his last cigarettes, and when his bicycle was whole again he wobbled off down the valley waving without looking back, which is, I have come to believe, the correct and only way to leave people you have loved briefly and well.

The procession came down the narrow street before I knew it was coming, announced first by drums I felt in my chest and then by a wall of marigold smell, and then the float itself, the god swaying on the shoulders of forty straining men. The crowd pressed me to the wall and I let it; there was nowhere to be but inside this. Petals fell from balconies. A grandmother beside me wept openly, and I, who believed none of it, found my own eyes stinging.

For three days the town belonged to the festival, and the festival belonged to no one in particular, which is what made it a festival. Strangers pressed sweets on me. A man I had never met taught me the steps of a dance everyone but me already knew. At night the square filled with lanterns and the band played until the players themselves were swaying, and I went to bed each dawn having understood nothing and enjoyed everything.

The penitents walked barefoot over the hot stones, hooded, carrying the great weight of the saint, and the crowd hushed as they passed and then released its held breath into applause. I had stumbled into a grief I did not share and a faith I did not hold, and yet the seriousness of it reached me. Whatever this town was mourning and celebrating at once, it was doing so with its whole body, and that is rarer than belief.

Holi caught me unprepared, as it is designed to, and within an hour of leaving my room I was every colour at once, magenta in the hair, green to the elbows, abandoned utterly to the joyful violence of it. Children ambushed me from doorways. An old man solemnly anointed my forehead with blue and then grinned like a boy. By evening the whole city looked tie-dyed and exhausted and entirely, helplessly happy.

The lantern festival sent its lights up from the river at dusk, hundreds of them, then thousands, each carrying a wish I could not read written by a hand I would never know. They rose unevenly, the way hope does, some catching and climbing, some failing into the water. I bought one from a girl on the bank and let it go, and watched it join the slow gold migration upward until I genuinely could not tell my light from the rest.

Carnival did not so much begin as overflow, the ordinary streets I had walked all week suddenly unrecognisable under feathers and sequins and a noise that had mass. I was swept along in it, a drab figure in a moving garden, and gave up resisting and let the parade decide my direction. Somewhere a drumline kept the whole city's pulse. I did not understand the costumes or the songs and it did not matter; the body understands a celebration.

The fishing village blessed its boats once a year, and on that morning the whole harbour was dressed with flags and the priest went from vessel to vessel with holy water and a few practised words. The fishermen stood bare-headed and serious, men who feared little, asking the sea politely for another year of mercy. Afterwards there was wine on the quay, and the seriousness dissolved into laughter, but I had seen it, the older thing beneath.

I arrived in the town on the eve of its patron saint's day and was therefore unable to find a room, a meal, or a sober local, and so the festival simply absorbed me. A family fed me because I was there and hungry. A band played me down a street I had not meant to walk. The fireworks, when they came, lit the cathedral and ten thousand upturned faces, mine among them, all of us briefly and equally astonished.

The harvest procession wound up from the fields with the last sheaf carried high, plaited into the shape of a woman, and the village walked behind it singing a song that was clearly older than the church it ended at. I followed at the back, an outsider at a rite, and felt the particular ache of witnessing a thing you cannot inherit. They had been doing this since before my country was a country, and would, I hoped, be doing it long after.

On the night of the dead the cemetery filled with candles and families and picnics, and the line between mourning and party dissolved into something gentler and wiser than either. Children played among the graves. An old woman tended a stone with the tenderness of someone making a bed. I walked the lit paths feeling neither sad nor intrusive, only grateful to be shown a country's clear-eyed friendship with its own grief.

The ferry pulled away from the mainland into a swell that took a few passengers green, and I stood at the stern watching the harbour shrink and the gulls give up the chase one by one. Ahead, the island was a low blue smudge that took two hours to become a place. When it finally resolved into houses and a church and a man on the jetty waiting for someone, I felt the small clean thrill that only an island arrival gives.

The coast road climbed and fell with the cliffs, and at every bend the sea offered a different argument: here a cove of impossible turquoise, there a grey churn against black rock. I drove it slowly, stopping too often, because a coastline asks to be read slowly. A fishing boat worked the swell far below, leaving a thread of wake, and the whole afternoon smelled of salt and gorse and warm tarmac.

I waited for the ferry in a café where the tide was the only clock anyone consulted, and the woman behind the counter could tell from the colour of the water how rough the crossing would be. Rough, she said, and was right. The boat bucked the channel for forty minutes while a small dog skidded the length of the deck and a child laughed at every lurch, and I held the rail and grinned and was, briefly, ten years old.

The fishing harbour emptied at four in the morning and filled again at noon, and in between the village simply waited, mending nets, drinking coffee, watching the horizon for its own boats. I sat on the wall through one of these intervals and understood that the whole place was organised around an absence and its hoped-for end. When the first hull rounded the breakwater the village exhaled, and a dozen women started walking, unhurried, down to the quay.

We crossed at dusk and the sea went through every colour it owns, pewter to rose to a final ink, while the lighthouse on the headland began its patient sweep. The ferry's engines made the deck tremble underfoot. A man beside me said he made this crossing twice a week and still came up on deck for the lighthouse, every time, because some things, he said, you should refuse to get used to.

The path along the cliff edge had been walked into the turf by centuries of feet, and it dipped to every cove and rose to every headland with the logic of someone who had all day. Below, the sea worked at a stack of rock it would, in some unimaginable year, finally bring down. I ate my lunch with my legs hanging over a drop, and the wind tried gently to take my hat, and I let it think it might.

The inter-island ferry was really a workboat that took passengers as a favour, and it called at jetties so small they were sometimes only a ladder against a rock. Crates of supplies went off, sacks of mail, a new washing machine roped upright. At one island a single old man boarded with a single suitcase, going somewhere or leaving somewhere, and the sea between the islands held us all in its blue indifference and carried us anyway.

Storm-bound, the ferry sat in harbour for two days, and the island it served and the mainland it left both simply waited, joined and separated by the same weather. I walked the harbour wall in the wind, watching the swell explode white against the light, and felt the particular peace of having my plans cancelled by something so much larger than my plans. When the boat finally sailed the sea was glassy, apologetic, and unbelievably calm.

The beach went on for miles with no one on it but me and the long lines of weed the tide had drawn and redrawn, and the cliffs at its back held the heat and gave it slowly down. I walked until the village behind me was a rumour and the village ahead was a guess, in that long blank middle of a coast where you meet only the sea and your own footprints, and both of them are good company.

We sailed into the fjord and the cliffs closed around the ship until the sky was a blue ribbon directly overhead, and waterfalls came down the rock walls in white threads from snowfields we could not see. The water was black and so still it doubled everything. No one on deck spoke above a murmur. The scale of it made conversation feel like litter, and so we all just stood and looked, which was the only sensible response.

subtopic: the smell and texture of place
sentence: Every city announces itself first to the nose, and this one was woodsmoke and frying garlic and the green river smell of a canal, all braided together and unmistakable. I could have found my way back to my room by scent alone, turning at the bakery, again at the tannery I learned to breathe shallowly past, and into the lane where a jasmine had been allowed to overrun a wall and forgave the street everything.

subtopic: the smell and texture of place
sentence: The heat here was not weather but a substance, something you pushed through, something that got into the seams of your clothes and the back of your thoughts. By noon the streets were given over to dogs and shadow, and the whole town held its breath behind shutters. I learned to move at the town's pace, to surrender the middle of the day, and found in that enforced stillness a luxury my own busy country had never offered me.

subtopic: the smell and texture of place
sentence: The cold in that mountain town had an edge you could almost hear, a fine high ringing in the ear, and the air was so thin and clean it seemed to have been rinsed. Smoke rose from the chimneys dead straight. The cobbles struck back hard through the soles of my boots. Everything was sharpened, defined, slightly painful, and after the soft blur of the lowlands it felt like being woken from a long and pleasant doze.

subtopic: the smell and texture of place
sentence: Rain in that country was not an event but a climate, a constant soft conversation between sky and ground, and within a day I had stopped noticing it and within two I had started to love it. It greened everything, dripped from every eave, beaded on the wool of every sheep, and made the indoors, when you reached it, a small triumph of orange light and steam and the smell of wet dog and woodsmoke.

subtopic: the smell and texture of place
sentence: The market quarter was a single overwhelming texture, a press of cloth and copper and skin, of hands on your sleeve and voices in your ear and the slick of fish water underfoot. There was no still point in it and no silence. I learned to read it the way you learn to read surf, to find the rhythm and ride it, and after an hour of resistance and an hour of surrender I came out the far side exhilarated and somehow rinsed.

subtopic: the smell and texture of place
sentence: The desert town smelled of dust and diesel and, surprisingly, of mint, because every café kept it in jars and bruised it into tea all day long. The light was a hammer. The shade, when you found it, was a kind of mercy you could taste. At dusk the heat lifted off the sand in a visible shimmer and the whole town came outside to sit on its low walls and watch the day go, and I sat with it.

subtopic: the smell and texture of place
sentence: Underfoot the city changed every few steps: the worn marble of the old quarter, slick and faintly treacherous; the rough setts of the artisans' lane; the warm soft tar of the new road by the river. I came to know the place through my soles before my eyes caught up, and could tell, walking back blind-drunk one night, exactly where I was by the texture of the ground, like a hand reading braille.

subtopic: the smell and texture of place
sentence: The port smelled of tar and rope and a fish-and-salt foundation that no amount of fresh paint would ever cover, and I found I did not want it covered. It was an honest smell, a working smell, the smell of a place that did something rather than merely posed for photographs. I breathed it deliberately, the way you might press a flower in a book, so that I could open it again, later, far inland, and be returned.

subtopic: the smell and texture of place
sentence: Spring came to the northern town all at once, as if a decision had been made, and overnight the air filled with the green wet smell of melt and the sound of water running everywhere, in gutters, off roofs, under the last grey ribs of snow. The whole place seemed to creak and loosen. People stood in doorways with their faces tilted up, drinking the change, and a stranger smiled at me for no reason except that the season had turned.

subtopic: the smell and texture of place
sentence: The monsoon broke while I was in the bazaar, and the first fat drops on the dust released a smell so particular and so longed-for that the whole crowd stopped to breathe it in, sellers and buyers alike, faces lifted. Then the rain came in earnest and we all crammed under the awnings, strangers shoulder to shoulder, watching the lane turn to a river, the heat finally and gratefully broken, the air for the first time in months delicious.

I had no map of the old town and did not want one, and so I let the lanes decide, turning toward whatever looked most promising: a strip of sun, a smell of bread, an arch with green behind it. I got thoroughly lost within twenty minutes and stayed lost, contentedly, for hours, and found in that surrender a version of the city no guided route would ever have shown me, the city as it is when no one is performing it.

The best afternoons are the ones with no destination, when you put the map away and walk on the principle that any direction is the right one because all of them are unknown. I did this in a city whose name I will keep, and was rewarded with a courtyard of cats, a man repairing accordions, a view I could never find again, and the particular lightness that comes of being, for a few hours, genuinely and happily without a plan.

Lost in the medina, I stopped fighting it and started enjoying it, the way the lanes folded into each other, the way a doorway opened onto a workshop of brass and then a workshop of leather and then, impossibly, a garden. A boy offered to guide me out and I declined; being out was not the point. I had paid for a plane and a room precisely so that I could afford to be this productively, this gorgeously, lost.

I took the small road on purpose, the one the signs did not bother with, and it led me through villages too minor for the guidebook and along a river the maps treated as an afterthought. Nothing happened, which was the gift of it. An old man waved. A dog ran beside the car for a hundred metres. I arrived nowhere in particular by evening, and it had been one of the best days of the trip.

Getting lost in a foreign city is the cheapest adventure there is, and I have made a discipline of it: pick a tram at random, ride it to the end, and walk home. This one took me to a suburb of allotments and washing lines and a startled, ordinary life, and I walked back through it for two hours, unhurried, an explorer of nothing, mapping a district that wanted nothing from me and gave me everything.

I let myself get lost in the bazaar deliberately, because the bazaar is built to lose you, its logic radial and secret, and to fight it is to miss it. So I drifted. I followed copper sounds and then dye smells and then a cool draught of unexplained air, and surfaced eventually into daylight in a square I had not known existed, blinking, happy, and entirely unable to say how I had got there.

The hill town was a single staircase that branched, and I climbed it by whim, taking the left turn here for no reason and the right there for the look of a cat sunning itself. There is no being lost in such a place, only a slower kind of arriving. I came out on the roof of the town with the valley laid below me and could not have retraced a single step, and would not have wished to.

I missed my stop on the country bus, on purpose, just to see where the rest of the route went, and it went to a town with a name like a sigh and a square with one café and an enormous, useless, beautiful church. I drank a coffee, read the war memorial, watched the afternoon, and caught the bus back, and the detour, which cost me an hour and a few coins, is the part of the day I remember.

There is a particular pleasure in walking out of a town in no direction, simply away, until the houses thin and the fields begin and you are nowhere, on a road that goes somewhere you do not need to reach. I did this on my last evening, walked into the soft fields until the town was a glow behind me, and stood in the dark feeling the whole anonymous country breathing around me, and then walked back.

I had a free day and spent it lost, which is the only correct use of a free day in a strange city. I followed a canal because canals always go somewhere, and a church bell because bells gather people, and a smell of coffee because it never lies. By dusk I was footsore and could not have placed myself within a mile, and felt I had finally, properly, met the place.

We left before dawn to beat the heat, and the desert at that hour was a country of long blue shadows that shortened as we drove until, by ten, there were no shadows at all and the dunes burned white. The driver navigated by landmarks I could not see and rhythms I could not feel. At the well at noon we found three other vehicles and an unspoken brotherhood of people who understood that out here you stop, you share water, you ask after the road ahead.

The dunes were the colour of a lion and moved like slow water, and the wind kept rubbing out our tracks behind us so that we seemed always to be the first people ever to cross. At the top of each ridge there was another, and another, the horizon a series of held promises. When the sun went down the sand turned to embers and then to ash, and the cold came in like a tide, and the stars were so many they frightened me.

The road across the salt pan was simply a direction, a faith that if you kept the wheel straight you would, in some hours, reach the far shore of this dry white sea. The flatness undid all sense of scale; a distant truck might be a mile off or ten. We stopped once, and the silence pressed on the ears, and when I clapped my hands the sound went out and out and never came back, swallowed by all that nothing.

The oasis appeared exactly as the books promise an oasis to appear, a sudden disorderly green in all the disciplined gold, palms and a pool and the unmistakable music of running water. We had been two days in the dry, and the change was almost too much for the senses. I put my hands in the water and held them there, and a boy laughed at me, and I did not care, because the desert teaches you what water is.

By the third day of the crossing the desert had stopped being a landscape and become a condition, a thing happening to me rather than around me. The mind goes quiet out there; there is so little to process that the usual chatter simply runs out of fuel. I found I was thinking nothing at all, just driving, just being carried across the great blank page of it, and it was the closest I have come to peace.

The camels knew the way better than the men, and the men knew this and let them, and so our small caravan moved across the erg with a kind of pooled and ancient confidence. At dusk we made camp in the lee of a dune, and the cameleers brewed tea over a fire of dry brush and sang something low and endless, and the camels folded their legs and sat like furniture, and the desert turned the colour of dark honey.

Heat haze made the far mountains float and tremble, detached from the earth, and the track ran toward them for hours without bringing them nearer. The desert is honest about distance in a way no other landscape is; it shows you the whole impossible width of what you must cross and dares you to begin. We began. We always begin. And the mountains, late in the day, finally consented to come down and meet the ground.

We ran low on water on the second afternoon and the mood in the vehicle changed without anyone speaking, a tightening, a new attention to the fuel gauge and the sun. The desert does this; it strips travel down to its oldest terms. When we reached the well and it had water, the relief was physical, a loosening of something I had not known was clenched, and we drank and laughed too loudly and were, for an hour, gloriously alive.

At night the desert gave back the day's heat slowly through the sand, and I lay on it as on a cooling stove, watching satellites cross a sky so crowded with stars it had texture, like sand itself. A jackal called once, far off. The driver slept the instant sleep of a man who trusted the place. I lay awake a long while, not from fear but from a kind of greed, not wanting to miss any of it.

The wind got up in the afternoon and the horizon went the colour of a bruise, and the driver pulled a scarf across his face and told me to do the same, and then the sandstorm was on us, hissing and total. We sat it out for an hour in a stinging brown twilight, the vehicle rocking, the world reduced to the cab. When it passed the desert was utterly remade, every dune in a new place, and the silence afterward rang.

The cargo boat took passengers as ballast and we slept on deck among the sacks of rice, the great brown river carrying us downstream at the pace of the country itself. Villages slid past, each one a jetty and a cluster of stilted houses and children who ran the length of the bank waving. The captain steered by reading the water's surface, the swirls and slicks that marked the sandbars, a skill that looked like idleness and was the opposite.

We went up the river for three days and the jungle came down to drink at both banks, dense and dripping and loud at dusk with a thousand things calling at once. The boat's engine was the only straight line in all that tangle. At night we tied up to a tree and the dark closed in absolute, and the river kept moving beneath us, patient and enormous, going where it had always gone.

The canal boat moved at the speed of a walk, which is the correct speed for seeing a country, and I spent whole afternoons on its roof watching England unspool: a heron, a pub, a lock with its slow theatre of rising water, a field of cows that turned to watch us pass with mild communal astonishment. Nothing was urgent. The journey was the destination, literally, and I have rarely been so unhurriedly content.

The delta was a labyrinth of channels and the boatwoman knew every one, poling us through corridors of mangrove where the water was the colour of strong tea and crabs scuttled the exposed roots. Markets happened on the water here, life happened on the water, and I understood that to these people the river was not an obstacle the road had to cross but the road itself, the oldest and the only one that mattered.

The ferry up the great lake was a floating village in itself, families camped on the lower deck with their cooking fires and their goats, traders, students, a wedding party. For two days we crossed water so wide the far shore was a guess, and the boat became a small society with its own rhythms of meals and prayers and sleep, and I, who had boarded a stranger, disembarked feeling I had been somewhere as much as gone somewhere.

We took the slow boat because the fast boat is a stupidity, a way of converting a river into a corridor, and the slow boat is a way of letting the river be a river. It stopped where it liked. It drifted. The Mekong went amber in the evenings and the children on the banks were the same children, it seemed, all the way down, and by the end I could not have said where one day's water ended and the next began.

The barge carried timber and, incidentally, me, and the bargee and his wife fed me from their own pot and gave me the spare bunk and asked, in return, only company. We went down through the locks of the old industrial waterway, past mills now silent and towpaths now walked only by dog-owners, and the bargee named each one and what it had once made, a whole vanished economy recited from the tiller of its last working boat.

Dawn on the river was mist, the kind that lay on the water in a waist-deep blanket so that the boats seemed to be sailing through cloud, their lower halves erased. Fishermen worked their nets in this whiteness, half-visible, calling to one another in a language the fog seemed to soften. Then the sun got a grip on it and lifted it in tatters, and the river was suddenly there again, brown and ordinary and going about its day.

The river was the spine of the country and the boat its slow blood, and along it I watched the land change its mind: jungle to farmland to the first grey suburbs to, at last, the city itself, announcing itself in cranes and smoke and a quickening of the river traffic. To arrive at a city by water is to arrive the way it was built to be arrived at, from the front, by its oldest door.

We poled into the flooded forest where the wet season had drowned the trees to their crowns, and the boat slid between trunks in green underwater light, fish moving below us through what had lately been somebody's garden. The whole world had gone amphibious. A man paddled past us with his shopping. The forest did not seem distressed by its drowning; it had clearly done this before, every year, forever, and would do it again.

The town sat at four thousand metres and I arrived breathless, every staircase a negotiation, the thin air a constant quiet reminder of where I had come to. The light up here was merciless and pure, and the colours under it seemed to vibrate. People moved slowly, and I learned to move slowly with them, and found that the altitude, which punished the body, somehow rewarded the eye, sharpening everything it took away the breath to look at.

Nothing grows easily this high, and so the town was a triumph of stubbornness, its terraces clawed from the slope, its single tree a kind of civic miracle that everyone seemed quietly proud of. The mountains stood around it like a council of elders. At night the cold was a serious matter, and the families gathered close to their stoves, and the stars, with no thick air to dim them, hung so low they seemed a part of the town's own lighting.

I had read that the heart works harder up here and I felt it, a constant low effort underlying everything, the body taxed simply by existing. The townspeople, born to it, watched the lowlander labour up their streets with a sympathy that was not unkind. The market was thin, the goods hard-won, and yet there was laughter in it, and music in the evenings, life insisting on itself in a place that gave it no encouragement at all.

The mining town clung to the mountain at an altitude that left visitors dizzy and locals unbothered, and the whole place tilted, every street a ramp, every house bracing against the slope. The thin cold air kept the colours clean and the distances deceptive. I drank coca tea against the headache and watched the miners come up at dusk grey-faced from the dark, into a town that was itself half in the sky.

At this height the weather was a personality, mercurial and immediate: sun, then a swift grey ambush of cloud, then snow in July, then sun again, all within an hour. The town had learned to take it without comment. Doors stood ready to be shut. Washing was an act of optimism. I came to admire the equanimity of a people who lived so close to the sky that the sky was practically a neighbour, and a moody one.

The road up to the town switched back on itself so many times that the valley floor stayed in view for an hour, dwindling, while the air thinned and the ears popped and the vegetation gave up by degrees: trees, then scrub, then only the tough grey cushions of high-altitude plants. And then the town, impossibly, a clutch of red roofs in all that grey, smoke rising straight up in the still cold air, people living where people should not be able to.

I spent my first day in the high town doing almost nothing, on the local advice, letting the body make its slow peace with the altitude, and so I sat in the square and watched. Old men played a board game with bottle caps. A procession of schoolchildren crossed in pairs. The mountains changed colour through the afternoon. It was the right way to arrive, slowly, at the pace the thin air insisted on, and I have used it ever since.

The town's church was the highest I had ever stood in, and the priest, a wiry old man unbothered by the altitude that had me gasping, told me his congregation had been praying at this height for four hundred years. The thin air seemed appropriate to prayer somehow, the sky so close, the breath so precious. Through the open door the mountains performed their slow theatre of light, and the priest, following my gaze, smiled and said nothing.

The hot springs were the town's true heart, and at dusk everyone went to them, the steam rising into the freezing air, bodies easing into water heated by the same volcanic violence that had thrust this whole improbable place into the sky. I lay in the heat with the cold on my face and the stars coming out, and beside me an old woman sighed with a contentment I entirely shared, and we soaked in companionable silence.

Leaving the high town, I felt the air thicken as the road descended, the body's burden lifting, the breath coming easy, and I was almost sorry. There had been a clarity up there, a stripped-down quality to existence at altitude, that the comfortable lowlands would now blur. I looked back once at the red roofs in their bowl of mountains, already a memory, already improbable, and went down into the easier, lesser air.

By the second week of the walk my body had stopped complaining and started simply working, and the days had taken on the shape of the route: rise, walk, eat, walk, sleep, the whole of life reduced to a clean and ancient simplicity. The path had been walked for a thousand years and I could feel it, the groove of all those feet, and I added mine to the total and felt, for once, properly small in the best way.

The pilgrims came in all conditions, the devout and the broken and the merely curious, and the path made no distinction, asking the same blisters of everyone. I had set out for no clear reason and found, somewhere around the third hundred kilometres, that the reason was the walking itself, the meditative monotony of it, the way it emptied the mind of everything but the next ridge and the next village and the slow accumulation of distance into meaning.

Each night the pilgrim hostel filled with the same weary fellowship, feet bandaged, packs propped, the day's complaints traded like currency, and each morning we scattered along the route at our different paces only to gather again, the same faces, at the next refuge. It was the loosest possible community and one of the truest I have known, bound by nothing but a shared direction and a shared and gradual transformation.

I walked into the holy city at the end of a month on the road, footsore and changed, and the great shrine that the path had been aiming at all along rose up exactly as promised. The other pilgrims around me wept or fell silent or simply stopped, and I felt the journey close like a book. Whatever I had come to find, I had found it not at the shrine but in the walking, and the shrine knew it, and forgave me.

The way-markers were the whole conversation the path had with you, a painted arrow here, a cairn there, a worn old sign pointing into a wood, and learning to read them became a kind of trust, a daily small faith that the route knew where it was going. I followed them for weeks across a country, handed from marker to marker like a parcel, and was never once, in the end, betrayed.

There is a particular tiredness at the end of a long walking day that is not like any other tiredness, a clean depletion, a body that has been honestly used, and the meal that follows it tastes the way no other meal tastes. I learned to walk for that tiredness and that meal, and for the sleep after, dreamless and total, and for the morning when the body, against all reason, was somehow ready to do it all again.

The path went over a high pass on the fortieth day, and at the top there was a cairn that every pilgrim before me had added a stone to, a slow monument built by tired hands, and I chose my stone with unexpected care and set it on the heap. The wind took my breath. Below, the route fell away toward a haze that hid the rest of the journey, and I stood a while, between halves, and then went down.

I had thought I was walking to a place and discovered I was walking to a self, that the route was less a line on a map than a slow machine for changing the person fed into it. The pilgrim who would arrive was not the one who had set out; the walking had quietly disassembled and rebuilt him, kilometre by kilometre, and the shrine at the end was only the place where you were finally allowed to notice.

The villages along the pilgrim route had been receiving walkers for centuries and had a practised, weathered kindness about it, a fountain placed just where the thirst would peak, a bench in just the right shade. The locals waved without stopping their work. We were not events to them; we were weather, a seasonal flow of footsore strangers, and there was a comfort in being so gently and so thoroughly expected.

On the last morning I walked the final kilometres slowly, deliberately, not wanting the route to end, aware that I was about to lose the simple shape it had given my days. The cathedral towers came up over the trees. Other pilgrims passed me, hurrying to be finished; I let them. The path had been the gift, not the arrival, and I wanted to be on it, still walking, for as long as the road would let me.

I found the stall by the queue, which is always the right way to find a stall, and joined the locals waiting for a woman who had been making one dish, only one, at that corner for thirty years. She did not look up. The dish, when it came, was a paper bowl of something fried and herbed and impossibly good, eaten standing on the pavement, and I understood that I had just had the best meal of the trip and it had cost me less than a coffee.

The night market was a corridor of smoke and sizzle, every few metres a new fire, a new wok, a new transaction of small money for great pleasure. I ate my way down it slowly, a skewer here, a dumpling there, a glass of something pressed and sweet, and the vendors called their wares in a singsong that was half advertisement and half lullaby, and the whole hot crowded lane smelled like the inside of an appetite.

The cart sold one thing, a flatbread folded around a filling the man assembled with a conjuror's economy of motion, and a small crowd had gathered simply to watch him work. He griddled, he folded, he wrapped, he handed across, and turned to the next, never hurrying, never pausing, a craftsman at the height of an art the world would never call an art. I ate mine watching him, and the watching was half the meal.

I asked a taxi driver where he ate and he took me, with a detour and no extra charge, to a stall under a bridge where the soup had no name on any sign because everyone who needed to know already knew. I sat on a plastic stool and was handed a bowl, and it was the kind of food that explains a city, that tells you in one mouthful what the place values, what it considers comfort, what it has always done well.

The grandmother at the corner stall had a face like a walnut and hands that never stopped, and she fed half the neighbourhood from a single charcoal grill, knowing every regular's order without asking. I became, over a week, a minor regular myself, and on the last day she added something extra to my plate, a small wordless gift, and would not say what it was, and it was delicious, and I have wondered ever since.

Breakfast in that city was a thing you ate walking, bought from a window, a hot parcel of dough and egg pressed into your hand by someone who had been awake since four, and the whole working population moved through the dawn streets eating it, a city feeding itself on the move. I joined the flow, parcel in hand, and felt, for the length of that breakfast, entirely and happily a local.

The fish was grilled on the quay where it had been landed an hour before, and the man who cooked it had also, very probably, caught it, and there is a freshness in that short journey from sea to plate that no restaurant can manufacture. I ate it with my fingers off a sheet of paper, looking at the boat it had come from, and the simplicity of the whole transaction felt like a kind of truth.

I did not know what I was ordering, pointed at a steaming pot because the woman beside me had pointed at it, and received a bowl of something I still cannot name and would happily cross the world to eat again. Street food rewards this kind of faith. The best meals of my travelling life have all been things I could not have ordered, because I did not have the words, and so I trusted, and the trust was repaid.

The market's food court was not a court and had no menus, just a horseshoe of stalls and a press of stools and a great communal cloud of fragrant steam, and you ordered by gesture and ate by elbow, shoulder to shoulder with strangers all engaged in the same urgent happy business. Nobody lingered and nobody hurried; the place had a rhythm, and you found it, and were briefly part of the city's appetite.

Late at night the only thing open was a single cart with a single lamp, and the man running it served a soup that seemed designed precisely for the hour and the cold and the loneliness of being abroad after dark. A few other night people gathered to it, a taxi driver, a nurse off shift, and we ate in the small pool of lamplight without speaking, fellowship enough in the shared bowl and the shared late hour.

I reached the ruined city in the early light before the buses, and for an hour it was mine, the toppled columns and the grass-grown amphitheatre and the temple still somehow standing, all of it silent except for birds. To be alone in such a place is to feel time as a physical pressure. I sat in the empty theatre where ten thousand had once sat, and the silence where their voices had been was the loudest thing I have heard.

The temple had been swallowed by the forest and then, painstakingly, recovered from it, and the great roots still gripped the stones like the forest's reluctant signature on the lease. I walked the long causeway in the heat with the carvings unrolling beside me, kings and gods and battles, a whole civilisation's idea of itself in stone, and felt the particular vertigo of standing in the achievement of a people entirely gone.

Nothing remained of the town but its outline in the turf, the streets visible as shallow channels, the houses as faint rectangular ghosts, and a single standing arch the centuries had not quite managed to bring down. I walked what had been the main street with the sheep that grazed it now, and tried to people it, to hear the market, and could not, and the failure was itself a kind of knowledge.

The pyramids were not what I expected, which is what everyone says and is nonetheless true; the photographs had not prepared me for the sheer obstinate mass of them, the way they sat on the desert as if they had grown there. I put my hand flat on a block bigger than a car and thought of the hand that had set it, four thousand years gone, and the stone, sun-warm, seemed to carry the heat of that vanished afternoon.

The rock-cut tombs glowed pink at sunset, the whole carved valley taking the low light and holding it, and I walked the floor of it as the shadows climbed the cliffs, among facades a vanished people had cut from the living rock as a way of arguing with death. They had lost the argument, of course; everyone does. But the arguing was magnificent, and it was still here, still beautiful, still saying something to the dusk.

The monastery had been abandoned for centuries and the mountain had been slowly taking it back, the cloisters open to the sky, a fig tree growing where the altar had been. I sat in the roofless church and the silence had a quality, a residue, as if all the prayers said here had left a faint warmth in the stones. Perhaps they had. Perhaps that is what ruins are: places where something accumulated and was then, very slowly, released.

The hill fort was just a series of grass ramparts now, concentric and enormous, the work of a people who left no writing and so no name, and I climbed the rings of it in the wind feeling the deep strangeness of an effort so vast and a purpose so lost. They had moved a mountain of earth to be safe. They were not safe. Nobody is. And yet the ramparts held the hill, beautiful and pointless and moving.

I climbed to the citadel as the heat went out of the day, and the ruined walls took the evening colour, and below me the modern town went about its evening, oblivious, built from the citadel's own fallen stones. There is a continuity in such places that the word ruin fails to catch; nothing here had really ended, only changed address. The old city had not died. It had simply moved downhill and learned to use electricity.

The standing stones stood as they had stood for five thousand years, on a moor that gave no other clue to their meaning, and I walked among them in a thin rain feeling the enormous patience of stone. Whoever raised them had a reason urgent enough to move rock the size of a house. The reason was gone. The rock remained. And the gap between the two, the lost why of it, was the most haunting thing on that whole grey moor.

The buried city had been dug from the ash that killed it, and to walk its streets was to walk through an interrupted afternoon, a loaf still in an oven, a dog still at the end of a chain, a graffito still fresh on a wall. The catastrophe had preserved what it destroyed. I stood in a kitchen two thousand years cold and felt, more sharply than in any cemetery, the simple unbearable fact that these had been people, exactly like me, who had not expected the day to end.

We had been told the elephants used this waterhole at dusk and we waited for them in the heat-thick light, and when they came it was without sound, an enormous grey procession simply assembling at the water as if condensed from the air. The matriarch drank and watched us watching her and decided we were nothing, and the whole herd relaxed, and a calf rolled in the mud, and we sat in the vehicle holding our breath at the privilege of being ignored.

The whale surfaced beside the boat without warning, a long black island of muscle rising and rising, and the smell of its breath hung over us, briny and ancient, before it rolled and showed an eye the size of a fist that took us in, considered us, and was unimpressed. Then it sounded, the great flukes lifting and sliding under, and the sea closed over a creature next to which our boat had felt, suddenly, like a toy.

At dawn the forest was a wall of sound, every bird and insect and unseen thing announcing itself, and the guide stopped and held up a hand, and through the green a troop of monkeys was moving, unhurried, overhead, dropping fruit and indifference in equal measure. We stood beneath them, craning, and one paused to look down at the upturned pale faces, and there passed between us a moment of mutual and entirely honest curiosity.

The leopard was in the tree before we saw it, draped along a branch with the boneless ease of a thing that owns the place, and the guide cut the engine and we sat in a silence so complete I could hear my own pulse. It watched us without lifting its head. There was no menace in it and no welcome either, only a vast feline calm, and I understood that we had been granted an audience and that it would end when the leopard, not we, decided.

The penguins came ashore in the evening in a small determined crowd, having spent the day at sea, and they walked up the beach past our quiet group with the busy self-importance of commuters, ignoring us utterly. To watch a wild animal go about its ordinary business, unbothered by your existence, is a rarer gift than to watch it perform; the penguins were not a spectacle, they were simply, gloriously, going home.

A fox crossed the path ahead of me in the grey of early morning and stopped, and we regarded each other across twenty feet of wet grass with a shared and total stillness. There was an intelligence in its yellow stare, an appraisal. Then it decided, flowed off the path into the bracken, and was gone, and I walked on absurdly pleased, carrying the encounter all day like a small warm coin in a pocket.

The reef under the snorkel mask was a city in full riot, fish in colours that seemed a kind of shouting, a turtle ploughing past with ancient patience, the coral itself alive and reaching. I floated above it for an hour, weightless, breathing through a tube, an awkward visitor to a world that managed its dazzling business with no reference to me whatsoever, and surfaced reluctant, blinking, returned to the dull dry country of air.

We tracked the gorillas uphill through nettles and mud for two hours, and then the guide froze, and there they were, a family at rest in a clearing, the silverback enormous and serene, a baby tumbling over its own limbs. We were allowed an hour. I spent it barely breathing, the camera forgotten, watching a creature so like us and so utterly itself look back at me with a calm that made all my hurry, my whole hurried species, seem suddenly absurd.

The migration crossed the river while we watched, ten thousand wildebeest pouring down the bank and into the current in a churning desperate flood, the crocodiles waiting, the dust and the noise and the sheer animal urgency of it almost too much to take in. It was not beautiful. It was something older and harder than beautiful. It was the planet doing what it has always done, indifferent and immense, and we were lucky beyond words to see it.

A heron stood in the shallows of the river all the long afternoon I watched it, motionless, a study in patience, and then in a movement too fast to follow it struck and had a fish, and went back to its stillness as if nothing had happened. I have thought about that heron often. It knew something about waiting, about the long boredom that precedes the necessary swift act, that I, a restless traveller, am still trying to learn.

subtopic: hot springs, baths, and bathing culture
sentence: The hammam was a series of marble rooms each hotter than the last, domes pierced with stars of coloured glass that dropped slow shafts of light through the steam, and an attendant scrubbed me with a coarse mitt until I felt I had shed a layer of the journey itself. Afterward I lay wrapped in cloth in the cooling room, drinking mint tea, hollowed out and gleaming, and understood that the bath here was not hygiene but ceremony.

subtopic: hot springs, baths, and bathing culture
sentence: The onsen sat in a gorge where the river steamed, and the bathing was outdoors, in stone pools at the snow's edge, the contrast of the scalding water and the freezing air a kind of exquisite shock. I soaked in silence, the etiquette here being one of quiet, and watched the steam rise and the snow fall into it and vanish, and felt the long road's tensions dissolve out of my shoulders into the volcanic, ancient warmth.

subtopic: hot springs, baths, and bathing culture
sentence: The thermal pool was the social centre of the village, and at the end of the day everyone came to it, the farmers and the children and the very old, and the talk in the steam was the day's news and the year's gossip and the slow unhurried business of a community keeping itself company. I lowered myself in among them, an obvious foreigner, and was absorbed without comment into the warm democratic water.

subtopic: hot springs, baths, and bathing culture
sentence: I followed the smell of sulphur up the mountain to where the spring broke from the rock, and someone, generations ago, had dammed it into a pool, and now it was simply a fact of the landscape, free, unsupervised, available. I soaked in it alone with the valley spread below, the water carrying up from the planet's hot interior a heat that felt almost personal, almost like care, and stayed until my fingers wrinkled and the light went.

subtopic: hot springs, baths, and bathing culture
sentence: The bathhouse was a tall echoing room of tile and steam, and the ritual was strict and silent: rinse, soak, rinse again, the body slowly opened and emptied by the heat. Old men sat submerged to the chin with their eyes closed, in a meditation that needed no name. I joined them, found the silence was not awkward but companionable, and left an hour later feeling I had attended a service in a religion that asked nothing but cleanliness.

subtopic: hot springs, baths, and bathing culture
sentence: The geothermal lagoon was an improbable blue against the black lava, milky and warm and faintly mineral, and people drifted in it under a low grey sky as if they had all been becalmed in the same pleasant dream. I floated on my back with the steam on my face and the cold rain falling into the warm water, and the strangeness of the planet's plumbing felt, for once, like an extravagant gift made personally to me.

subtopic: hot springs, baths, and bathing culture
sentence: In that country the evening bath was a non-negotiable institution, and the small inn heated its tub at dusk, and the act of soaking before dinner was as fixed as dinner itself. I came to look forward to it the way one looks forward to sleep, the hot water dissolving the day's walking, and to understand that a culture which builds such a pause into every single day knows something about being alive that my own hurried country has forgotten.

subtopic: hot springs, baths, and bathing culture
sentence: The spring fed a chain of pools down the hillside, each cooler than the one above, and the local practice was to start hot and descend, the body adjusting pool by pool, until you finished in water barely warmer than the river. I went down the chain at dusk with a dozen quiet strangers, and we did not speak, only soaked and descended and soaked, performing together an old slow choreography that the hill itself had designed.

subtopic: hot springs, baths, and bathing culture
sentence: The bath was wood and the water was hot beyond comfort and then, suddenly, exactly right, and through the small window I could see snow on the cedars and a single lantern swinging. The innkeeper had heated it for me alone. To be given a private hour in such water, after weeks on hard roads, was a kindness so complete that I lay there near tears, undone by warmth, by quiet, by the simple fact of being looked after.

subtopic: hot springs, baths, and bathing culture
sentence: The riverside hot pools were communal and unremarkable to the locals and astonishing to me, naturally hot water surfacing right at the cold river's edge so that you could move, with one step, between the planet's two temperaments. Families had been coming here for centuries; there were grooves worn in the rock by generations of the same act. I added my own soak to the long total, and felt time, for an hour, become a circle.

The bus was meant for thirty and carried sixty, plus crates of fruit, two goats, and a wedding's worth of folded chairs lashed to the roof, and it ground up the mountain road in second gear with a patience I came to find moving. Every passenger knew every other. The driver stopped for anyone who flagged him, and for lunch, and once simply to admire a view, and the journey took all day, and was, in the end, the destination.

I had the local bus to myself for the first hour and then it filled, stop by stop, with a whole region's worth of life: schoolchildren, a man with a ladder, two arguing brothers, a woman whose baskets smelled of the herbs they held. The bus became, briefly, a moving village. People got off where their lives were and got on where their lives were, and I, getting off nowhere in particular, envied them all their destinations.

The overnight bus showed a film at a volume that defeated sleep and took the mountain curves at a speed that defeated rest, and I sat gripping the seat in front and watching the headlights swing across drops I was glad I could not see clearly. By dawn we had survived it, as the driver had clearly always known we would, and the sunrise over the valley we had crossed in the dark felt like a personal reprieve.

The bus station at five in the morning was a small chaos of touts and engines and the smell of the first tea, and finding the right bus was a matter of shouting destinations and trusting the answers. Once aboard, wedged by my pack, I felt the particular settled calm of having committed to a direction. The bus would go where it went. My only job now, for the next nine hours, was to watch the country come.

The minibus filled and then, against all apparent physics, kept filling, until I had a stranger's child asleep on my shoulder and a stranger's chicken regarding me from a basket at my feet, and we were all of us packed into a single shared and jolting fate. There is an intimacy forced on you by such travel that the comfortable traveller never knows, and by the journey's end the strangers were no longer quite strangers.
