The road was unpaved for two hundred kilometres and the bus took it like a small boat in a swell, and the passengers rode the lurches with the unconscious skill of long practice, swaying as one. Dust came in at every window and settled on everything, on the fruit, on the babies, on me, and by the journey's end we were all the same red colour, a busload of strangers united by the road's indifferent paintwork.

We broke down in the early afternoon in the middle of a plain with no shade and no town, and the driver and his boy got under the bus while the passengers got out and arranged themselves philosophically along the verge. Nobody complained. Somebody produced food and shared it. The breakdown was simply a part of the journey, an interval, and when the engine caught two hours later we all climbed back aboard as if nothing had happened, because nothing had.

The bus climbed all morning and crossed the pass at noon, and the conductor, who had been collecting fares and gossip in equal measure, fell silent at the top, and so did everyone, because the view demanded it. Then we started down the far side into a new valley, a new climate, a new language on the signs, and the bus, which had felt all morning like a labouring animal, now ran free and easy down toward the warmer country.

The shared taxi would not leave until it was full, and so I sat in it for an hour in the heat of the rank, watching the seats fill one passenger at a time, the whole departure an exercise in collective patience. When at last the final fare squeezed in, a kind of cheer went round, and we pulled away, six strangers bonded by the wait, and the road opened ahead of us into the long bright afternoon.

I have come to love the long bus journey precisely for its tedium, the way the hours of nothing-much sand down the restless mind until it is smooth and empty and finally able to simply look. Out the window the country passed, ordinary and endless, a town, a field, a man on a bicycle, and I watched it all with the contented vacancy of a person who has, for nine unhurried hours, absolutely nowhere else to be.

I slipped into the cathedral out of the noon glare and the cool dark closed over me like water, the great space rising into shadow, a few candles burning, a single old woman at prayer. I am not a believer, but I sat in a back pew and let the silence work on me, the centuries-deep quiet that such places hoard, and came out twenty minutes later somehow rinsed, ready again for the bright loud city outside.

The monastery clung to a crag above the valley and the monks had lived their slow life there for a thousand years, and a guest could stay if a guest kept the silence. I stayed two nights. The bells divided the dark into offices. The food was plain and the cell was bare, and in the great hush between the prayers I found a quality of rest I had not known I was starving for, and left reluctantly, and changed.

The temple complex unfolded courtyard within courtyard, each one quieter than the last, the noise of the city filtering down to nothing, until in the innermost garden there was only the sound of a single bamboo pipe tapping water into a stone basin. I sat on the worn wooden veranda where pilgrims had sat for centuries and did nothing at all, and the doing of nothing, in that place, felt like the most purposeful thing I had done in months.

The mosque's courtyard was vast and cool and floored with stone worn smooth, and the faithful came and went in the soft rhythm of the prayer hours, and between those hours the great space held a silence so deep it felt like a presence. I sat against a pillar in the shade, removed my shoes as the custom asked, and let the calm of the place, which asked nothing of my own beliefs, simply be offered and simply accepted.

The little roadside shrine was nothing, a niche, a painted saint, a shelf for candles and the small gifts of passers-by, and yet someone tended it, someone kept the candles lit and swept the step, and I stopped at it the way you stop at any small evidence of care. Travellers had left things: a coin, a flower, a folded note. I left a coin too, for the company of the gesture more than the faith of it.

The pilgrimage church stood alone on its hill, and the climb to it was part of the prayer, and at the top there was wind and a view and a building full of the ex-votos of the grateful and the desperate: little painted plaques, crutches, photographs. It was a museum of human need and human hope, unbearably moving, and I stood among the offerings of strangers feeling the whole weight of how much, and how alike, people want.

The forest temple was reached by a flight of mossy steps under enormous cedars, and the trees themselves felt like the older religion, the temple a newcomer that had simply agreed with them. Lanterns lined the way, unlit in the daylight. The shrine at the top was small and the forest was vast, and it was clear which one the silence belonged to, and clear too that the temple had been wise enough to know it.

I went into the synagogue, one of the oldest in the country, and the caretaker, an old man with all the time in the world, walked me through its quiet rooms and told me its long story of flourishing and catastrophe and stubborn survival. The light came through high windows onto worn wood. He did not ask my faith and I did not offer it; he was simply glad, I think, to have someone to tell, and I was glad to be told.

The hilltop chapel was always unlocked, the priest told me, because a locked sanctuary is a contradiction, and so I let myself in at dusk to a single room, whitewashed, almost bare, a window framing the last light over the sea. I sat in it alone for an hour. Nothing happened, in the sense that the word usually means; and everything happened, in some other sense I have never found the words for, and have stopped trying to.

The great stupa was circled, all day and into the night, by a slow river of pilgrims turning prayer wheels, and the act was so constant and so old that the path around it had been worn into a groove. I joined the circle, not as a believer but as a body willing to be carried, and walked round and round in the murmuring crowd, and found that the simple repetition, the shared slow orbit, was its own kind of quiet.

I found a way onto the rooftop at dusk, and the whole city lay below me, a slow tide of lights coming on, the call to prayer rising from one minaret and then another until the sound was a net thrown over everything. The rooftops were their own country up here, hung with washing and water tanks and the occasional cat, and families had come up to sit in the cool, and I sat among them, an invited stranger to the city's quiet hour.

The hostel roof was the place everyone gathered as the heat went out of the day, a tangle of mismatched chairs and a view across a thousand flat roofs to the cathedral catching the last sun. Travellers traded plans and beers and the lies one tells about one's own bravery. Below us the city dimmed and glittered, and we watched it the way you watch a fire, saying less and less, until the dark was complete and someone fetched a guitar.

From the rooftop café the medieval town was a chaos of tiled roofs at every angle, none of them agreeing with another, swifts cutting through the gaps in screaming squadrons. I drank my coffee and read the skyline like a sentence: the cathedral, the clock tower, the ruined wall, the hills beyond. A city seen from above gives up its secret order, the logic the streets are too close to show.

I climbed the bell tower for the view and got it, the whole city spread in the gold evening, the river a bright thread stitching the districts together, the mountains a blue rumour at the edge. The bell, beside me, was the size of a small room. When it struck the hour I felt the sound in my teeth, in the stone, in the soles of my feet, and below me the city, used to it, did not even look up.

The flat roofs of the old quarter were a hidden second city, connected, it seemed, to each other more than to the streets below, and the women hung their washing and their conversations across the warm tiles in the evening. I had been given a roof to sleep on, and lay on it under a sky still pink, listening to the city talk to itself across the rooftops, a murmur that went on long after the streets had gone quiet.

The skyline at dawn was a slow act of revelation, the towers emerging from a violet haze one by one as the light strengthened, the river still holding the last of the night. I had climbed up here precisely for this, for the city before it was fully a city, before the noise, when it was just shapes and silence and the first slow movement of the day, and it gave me the morning as a gift before anyone else woke to claim it.

The rooftop bar charged too much and was worth it, because it sold a view: the city falling away in tiers of light to a dark harbour, ships moving on it slow as thoughts, the far shore a faint necklace of gold. I nursed one drink for an hour, which the city, in its glittering indifference, did not mind, and watched the planes come down over the bay in a patient luminous queue.

From above, the slum and the gleaming district were the same distance from the sky and so, for a moment, looked equal, the rooftops of corrugated tin and the rooftops of glass both simply catching the same sunset. The city was honest from up here in a way it was not at street level. I stood on the high terrace and watched it all glow indiscriminately, and the inequality I had walked through all day was, briefly, only light.

The minarets and the church towers and the one absurd modern skyscraper stood up out of the low brown sprawl like the city's argument with itself, each one a different century insisting on its own idea of height. I watched the sun set behind them from a rooftop garden, the call to prayer braiding with the church bells, and the city below carried on its evening, deaf to the long quarrel its own skyline was conducting overhead.

I had not known the city had so many roofs until I got above them, and then it was all roofs, a rumpled red and grey ocean of them stretching to the haze, dotted with the green of secret terraces and the white of satellite dishes turned all one way like a field of sunflowers. The streets, which had felt like the whole city, were revealed as mere cracks in this upper world, this airy untrodden country of the tiles.

The lake at first light was a sheet of mercury, so still it doubled the mountains exactly, and a single fisherman in a wooden boat hung suspended between the real peaks and their reflections, in the middle of a symmetry too perfect to seem real. I stood on the shore not wanting to move, not wanting even to breathe hard, in case the lake noticed and rippled, and broke the impossible mirror it was holding so patiently up to the sky.

The village faced the lake the way other villages face a square, the water its forum and its livelihood and its weather, and life proceeded along the shore at the unhurried pace of something that has been beside still water for a very long time. I rented a room with a window full of lake, and woke each morning to its flat grey patience, and felt my own restlessness slowly settle, like silt, to the bottom of me.

I rowed out onto the lake in the late afternoon and shipped the oars and simply drifted, and the silence was so total that I could hear, far off, a door close, a dog, a child, the whole shore's small life carried clean across the water. The boat turned slowly. The light went amber, then rose, then a deep blue, and I let the lake hold me through all of it, in no hurry at all to row back to being a person with plans.

The inland sea was so vast it had its own horizon and its own moods, and the lakeside towns called it the sea and meant it, and treated it with the wariness coastal people give the ocean. I walked its shore for a day and the far side never came into view. Gulls worked the shallows. It smelled, faintly and impossibly, of salt, and I understood that a body of water large enough simply becomes a sea, by acclamation, regardless of the maps.

Mist lay on the lake until mid-morning, and the village emerged from it slowly, a jetty first, then a roof, then the whole reflected shore, as if the day were being developed like a photograph. The fishermen went out into the whiteness and were swallowed, their oar-strokes audible long after they were gone. Then the sun took the mist and the lake lay revealed, blue and enormous and entirely calm, as if it had never been hiding anything at all.

The monastery sat on an island in the middle of the lake, reached by a boatman who had been ferrying pilgrims and the curious across for forty years and had stopped finding either remarkable. The crossing took half an hour of flat grey water. On the island the bells, the gardens, the quiet; and around it the lake, holding the small holy place apart from the world the way a hand cups a candle, and I was glad, crossing back, that some things are kept hard to reach.

I swam in the lake at dawn, the water cold enough to take my breath, and floated on my back in the middle of it watching the mist burn off the surrounding hills. There was no one. The lake was mine, briefly, the way nothing is ever really yours but a clear cold morning sometimes pretends to be, and I floated in the centre of that pretence until the cold drove me in, grinning, to a towel and the rising sun.

The lake town had a promenade and the promenade had benches, and the benches were occupied each evening by the same old men in the same order, watching the same water do the same nothing, and finding in it, clearly, an inexhaustible interest. I joined them. The water did nothing. The light changed on it slowly. And I began, by the end of the week, to understand the benches, and the old men, and the particular wealth of having a lake to do nothing in front of.

The reed beds at the lake's edge were loud at dusk with birds settling, a whole quarrelsome city of them coming home to roost, and then, abruptly, silent, and the lake gave back a sky going from gold to ash. A heron stalked the shallows. The water lapped the stones with a sound like slow breathing. I sat until the first stars showed, and the lake darkened, and held them too, doubling the sky as patiently as it had doubled the day.

The ferry crossed the lake twice a day and the lakeside villages arranged their lives around its horn, and I took it from end to end simply to be on the water, and watched the shore unscroll its terraced vineyards and its small stone churches and its bathing children. The lake was the country's quiet centre, the place its noise did not reach, and crossing it I felt the whole nation, for an hour, lower its voice.

subtopic: caravanserai, inns, and lodgings with history
sentence: The caravanserai had sheltered the camel trains for six centuries and now sheltered me, and the great courtyard, where bales had once been stacked and deals struck, held only the evening light and a single fig tree. My room had been a merchant's, the walls thick against the desert's two extremes. I lay in it listening to the silence where the bells of a thousand caravans had been, and felt myself a very minor entry in a very long ledger.

subtopic: caravanserai, inns, and lodgings with history
sentence: The inn had a name over the door and a date carved beneath it three hundred years old, and the floors sloped and the beams stooped and the whole building seemed to lean companionably toward the fire. Travellers had been warming themselves at this hearth since before my country was settled. The innkeeper showed me to a low-doored room and a deep bed, and I slept the sleep of all the tired strangers who had slept there before me.

subtopic: caravanserai, inns, and lodgings with history
sentence: The pilgrim hospice had been giving beds to walkers for eight hundred years, and the practice had worn the place into a particular shape, a courtesy worn smooth as the stone steps. A volunteer washed my feet, an old custom he performed without ceremony or comment, and gave me bread and a bunk in a long room of bunks. I lay there among strangers in the dark, one more pilgrim in an unbroken chain of them, and felt held by the sheer weight of the precedent.

subtopic: caravanserai, inns, and lodgings with history
sentence: The riad turned its back on the street, as the old houses do, and opened inward onto a courtyard of tiles and a fountain and a square of sky, and within its thick walls the city's heat and noise simply ceased to exist. The family who kept it had kept it for generations. I drank tea in the courtyard at dusk while swifts wheeled in the patch of sky overhead, and understood the deep wisdom of a house built around a quiet.

subtopic: caravanserai, inns, and lodgings with history
sentence: The coaching inn still had the wide arch the coaches had driven through and the yard they had wheeled in, though the coaches were two centuries gone and the yard held cars now. The bar had a fireplace big enough to roast in and a floor of flags worn into hollows. I drank a pint where the mail had once changed horses, and the building seemed to hold all its eras at once, indifferent to which century happened to be using it.

subtopic: caravanserai, inns, and lodgings with history
sentence: The guesthouse had been a noble's mansion and then a school and then a barracks and now, faded and gentle, took in travellers, and each of its lives had left a layer: a painted ceiling here, an institutional stair there, a bricked-up door that led nowhere anyone now remembered. My room had been, the owner thought, a library. I slept among the ghosts of its many purposes, and the building seemed glad, at last, to be doing something so simple as sheltering a tired stranger.

subtopic: caravanserai, inns, and lodgings with history
sentence: The mountain refuge had stood at the col since the first climbers came, and its visitors' books, kept in a row on a shelf, went back a hundred years, the same handwriting of exhaustion and joy in every decade. I added my line to the latest one. The hut had no luxuries and needed none; its luxury was the precedent, the long company of everyone who had ever been glad, as I was glad, to reach its door out of the weather.

subtopic: caravanserai, inns, and lodgings with history
sentence: The monastery still let rooms to travellers, as monasteries have always done, and the cell was bare and the bell was early and the food was taken in silence, and all of it had been arranged this way for so long that it no longer felt like rule but like rest. I stayed three nights in the old rhythm. The monastery asked nothing and gave a great deal, and what it gave, I came to feel, was simply the experience of a building that had stopped hurrying centuries ago.

subtopic: caravanserai, inns, and lodgings with history
sentence: The traveller's lodge on the old trade road had a courtyard, a well, and rooms ranged around an upper gallery, and it had been built for exactly the kind of person I was, the traveller with a horse to stable and a night to spend. The horses were gone. The shape of the welcome was not. I stood on the gallery in the evening and watched the gate, half-expecting, in that timeless courtyard, a string of camels to come in out of the dusk.

subtopic: caravanserai, inns, and lodgings with history
sentence: The inn was the oldest building in the village and had been an inn the entire time, and the landlord, whose family had run it for two centuries, told its history while he poured, a tale of floods and fires and one famous visiting poet. The fire had burned in that grate, he said, every winter since the inn began. I sat by it that cold night feeling the unbroken warmth of it, two hundred winters of the same fire, and was comforted in a way I could not quite explain.

The train delivered me into a city I knew nothing of, at an hour I had not chosen, and I stood for a moment on the concourse simply absorbing the shock of it: the new alphabet, the new smell, the particular pitch of a crowd speaking a language I did not have. Then I shouldered the pack and walked out into it, into the bright loud unknown, with the specific terror and joy that only a first hour in a strange city gives.

I arrived after dark, which is the wrong way to arrive, the city reduced to a confusion of lights and a taxi driver's monologue and the smell of something frying somewhere, and I went to bed having seen nothing and woke to a window full of a city entirely unguessed-at from the night before. Morning had assembled it: rooftops, a hill, a tower, a haze of smoke. The city had been there all along, waiting, while I slept beside it, ignorant.

The first walk in a new city is the only one of its kind, the streets all equally unknown, every corner a genuine question, and I gave myself to it that first morning, no map, no aim, just the city teaching me itself one block at a time. I learned the river. I learned the loud street and the quiet one. By dusk the city had become, in my private rough way, mine, and I would never again be able to see it fresh.

I came into the city by bus and it announced itself slowly, the way cities do, in a thickening of traffic and a rising of buildings, the country I had crossed all day giving way to the suburbs and then the suburbs to the centre. By the time the bus pulled in I had been watching the city assemble for an hour, and stepped down into it already half-acquainted, which is the small mercy the slow arrival grants.

The city overwhelmed me in the first ten minutes, as the great cities will, the scale and the noise and the sheer indifferent momentum of millions of people not waiting for me, and I stood against a wall and let it wash past until the panic passed and the wonder took its place. Then I set off into it, one careful pedestrian among the multitude, and the city absorbed me without noticing, which is the great gift a city gives the stranger: anonymity, and a place in the crowd.

I found my street by the third attempt, having shown the address to three strangers who each pointed with great confidence in three different directions, and the finding of it felt like a small graduation. The room was plain and the window looked at a wall, and yet it was mine, a fixed point at last in the unknown city, and I sat on the bed in the early dark feeling the specific deep relief of having, in a strange place, an address.

The city smelled of coffee and exhaust and a river, and the first thing I did, before the map, before the room, was to walk into it and let the smell and the noise and the strangeness wash through me, because the first hour is the only hour the city is purely itself, unsorted, unlabelled. I drank a coffee at a counter, watched the morning crowd, and felt the slow click of a new place beginning to become familiar.

I arrived knowing one word of the language and not even sure I had it right, and the city forgave me, as cities forgive the newly arrived, with pointed fingers and patient repetitions and the universal sign language of the lost. By evening I had a room, a meal inside me, and three new words, and the city, which had seemed at noon an impenetrable wall, had become by dusk a place with footholds, a place I could, slowly, begin to climb.

Stepping off the ferry I had the whole unknown city laid out before me in the morning light, climbing its hill, and I stood at the rail a moment before disembarking simply to look, to have it once as a stranger has it, entire and unexplored. Then the gangway, the crowd, the customs, and I was in it, no longer above it, and the city closed around me, and the long delicious work of learning it began.

The first night in a new city I always sleep badly, the unfamiliar sounds keeping a part of me on watch, the trams and the strange birds and the particular rhythm of a foreign traffic, and I lay awake learning the city by ear. By the third night the sounds had become a lullaby, the city's voice no longer alien, and I understood that I had crossed, in those three nights, the small invisible border between visiting a place and beginning, however briefly, to live in it.

We stopped at the roadside café because the driver knew it, and it was nothing, a tin roof and four tables and a woman at a stove, and it served the best lentils I ate in that whole country. The truckers stopped here; that was the recommendation. I sat with my plate watching the road and the dust and the slow turn of a ceiling fan, and felt the particular contentment of a good meal found by luck in the middle of nowhere.

The café sat at a bend in the mountain road precisely because the bend made everyone slow down, and so everyone stopped, and the place had become, without trying, the crossroads of the whole valley. I drank coffee on its terrace and watched the valley's traffic pause and gossip and move on. The owner knew every face but mine, and made a point, before I left, of knowing mine too.

We had not planned to stop in the town at all, but the car wanted water and so did we, and the town turned out to have a square, a fountain, an enormous shady tree, and a café under it that served a cake I have tried and failed to find again ever since. The best stops are the unplanned ones. The itinerary takes you to the famous places; the breakdown takes you to the real ones.

The petrol station on the desert road had a café attached, and the café had a cat and a card game and a kettle always on, and it was, for the drivers who crossed that emptiness, less a business than an oasis, a fixed warm point in all the blank. We stopped, and were absorbed into the card game, and left an hour later than we meant, and richer for it, the way an unplanned hour always leaves you richer.

The bus stopped for lunch at a roadside place that had clearly fed buses for decades, the menu fixed, the service swift, the whole operation tuned to the rhythm of arrivals and departures. We had twenty minutes. I ate fast, walked the verge, watched the driver smoke, and climbed back aboard, and the café receded, a place I would never see again and never quite forget, one of the thousand small rooms the road keeps for travellers.

I stopped at the café because it had a view and stayed because it had a grandmother, and she fed me beyond all reason and asked, in halting borrowed words, about my journey, and I told her, and she nodded as if my whole route had passed across her terrace before. Perhaps it had. The road went by her door. She had been watching travellers go by it, and feeding the ones who stopped, for the better part of a long life.

The roadside stall sold only tea and only one kind, brewed thick and sweet in a blackened pot, and the man who sold it had a bench and a tarpaulin and a clientele of everyone who passed. I stopped because everyone stopped. The tea was scalding and excellent. Around the bench the conversation was the road's conversation, distances and conditions and the price of fuel, and I sipped and listened and was, for one glass of tea, a local of the road.

We pulled over at a café that was really someone's front garden, tables set out among the chickens, and the family that lived there simply expanded, when travellers stopped, into hosts. The food came from the garden it was served in. A child practised English on me with shy persistence. We had meant to stop for ten minutes and stayed an hour, and drove on full and slightly dazed by the abundance of an entirely unplanned welcome.

The mountain café was the last building before the pass and the first after it, depending on your direction, and so it had become the place where every traveller braced for the climb or recovered from it. I recovered from it, on the terrace, with a coffee and an enormous slice of something, looking back at the road I had just driven. The café knew exactly what I needed. It had been needed by everyone who came over that pass, for years.

I stopped at the café for a reason I have forgotten and remember the café still: the oilcloth on the table, the calendar three years out of date, the radio playing something local and sad, the patient old man who brought my coffee and then sat back down to his own. Nothing happened there. It was simply a half hour, in the middle of a long day, of being still in a small ordinary room in a country not my own, and it was enough, and it was good.

The road to the pass climbed for two hours through air that thinned with every switchback, and at the top there was a cairn, a tattered string of prayer flags, and a cold so pure it felt like an idea rather than a temperature. Both valleys were visible from up there, the one I had left and the one I was going to, two different worlds joined by this one frozen saddle, and I stood between them in the wind feeling the strange power of a high place.

We crossed the pass in a snow flurry that came from nowhere, the road suddenly white, the drop beside it suddenly invisible and therefore, for a few minutes, bearable, and the driver took it slowly, humming. At the summit the flurry stopped as suddenly as it had come, and the far valley opened below us, green and warm-looking and impossibly distant, a promise the road would spend the next two hours patiently keeping.

The pass had been the only way through the range for as long as there had been people on either side of it, and the path that crossed it was worn into the rock by all the millennia of feet and hooves that had braved it. I walked up it slowly, breathing hard, and at the top found a small shrine, a place to give thanks, and understood why: to cross such a place was, in any century, an achievement, and the gratitude of the survivors had pooled here, on the cold summit, for a thousand years.

From the top of the pass I could see the road I had spent all morning climbing, looped below me like a dropped ribbon, and the road I had still to descend, looped the same way into the next valley, and between them, where I stood, the high cold hinge of the whole journey. A condor turned overhead, level with me, unbothered. I drank from my bottle and felt, briefly and intensely, the achievement of altitude.

The bus laboured up to the pass all morning, the engine straining, the passengers quiet, and at the top the driver stopped, and we all got out into the thin freezing brilliant air to stretch and to look. Both worlds were there, the dry brown valley behind, the green wet valley ahead, divided by the rock we stood on. Then the horn, and we climbed back in, and the bus tipped over the crest and began, with relief, to roll down.

The pass was closed by snow for half the year, and crossing it in the brief open season felt like slipping through a door that would soon be shut, the road still rimmed with the last white, the cold still sharp. At the summit the marker stone gave the altitude, a number high enough to explain the headache and the breathlessness and the strange clarity, and below, on the far side, the season was already further along, the valley greener, the door to a different climate held briefly ajar.

We reached the pass at dawn on purpose, to cross it before the day's cloud came up to hide the peaks, and we were rewarded: the whole range stood clear and gold around us, summit after summit, in an air so still and cold it rang. The road over the pass was empty. We had the roof of the country to ourselves for half an hour, and then the first cloud came up the valley like a slow grey tide, and we went down ahead of it.

The high pass was a different climate, a different vegetation, a different silence, and crossing it on foot took the whole of a hard day, the path zigzagging up scree to a notch in the skyline that never seemed to come nearer. And then it did come, abruptly, and I stepped through the notch and the wind hit me and the new valley fell away at my feet, and I sat down on a rock, spent and triumphant, on the literal high point of the trip.

The cairn at the pass had been built one stone at a time by travellers giving thanks for the crossing, and I understood the impulse the moment I reached it, breathless and cold and absurdly pleased with myself. I found a flat stone and set it on the heap, my small contribution to a monument made entirely of relief, and the wind streamed the prayer flags out flat, and the next valley waited, far below, in a haze of its own weather.

The pass connected two languages, two cuisines, two ways of building a roof, and the people on either side had been trading across its cold spine for centuries, and resenting and marrying each other, and the pass was their shared difficulty and their shared door. I crossed it westward and the world changed: the bread changed, the greetings changed, the shape of the church towers changed, all of it tipped over the one cold ridge into a different idea of how to live.

subtopic: photographing and trying to capture a place
sentence: I raised the camera to the market and then lowered it, because some scenes resist the rectangle, lose everything in the cropping: the smell, the noise, the press of bodies, the particular slant of the light through the awnings. I put the camera away and simply stood and watched, trying instead to fix it in the slower and more reliable film of memory, and I have the market still, whole, while the photographs I did take of lesser things have faded into anyone's photographs.

subtopic: photographing and trying to capture a place
sentence: The view demanded to be photographed and so I photographed it, dutifully, and then sat down and looked at it properly, with my own eyes, for a long time, because the photograph would only ever be a receipt, a proof that I had been here, and the looking was the actual having. The valley held its light. I memorised it on purpose, the long way, and the memory, years on, is sharper than any file.

subtopic: photographing and trying to capture a place
sentence: I tried for an hour to photograph the canyon and failed, as everyone fails, because the camera cannot hold the scale, cannot fit the silence in, cannot record the slow vertigo of all that depth. The pictures came out as pretty postcards of a thing that was not pretty but overwhelming. In the end I stopped trying, and just stood at the rim and let the canyon overwhelm me, which was, after all, the only honest way to receive it.

subtopic: photographing and trying to capture a place
sentence: An old man in the square saw my camera and posed for it, unasked, with great dignity, and I took the picture because he wished it taken, and it is one of the best I have, not because of the light or the composition but because of the small human transaction inside it, the stranger who wanted, for some reason of his own, to be remembered, and the traveller who was glad to do the remembering.

subtopic: photographing and trying to capture a place
sentence: The festival was a riot of colour built for the camera and yet the camera kept failing it, freezing the motion that was the whole point, silencing the drums, flattening the crowd's electric warmth into a still and lifeless brightness. I gave up and joined the crowd instead, and let the festival happen to me rather than through a lens, and what I carried away was not an image but a feeling, which is heavier and lasts longer and cannot be shown to anyone.

subtopic: photographing and trying to capture a place
sentence: I have a photograph of the village and it tells almost none of the truth: not the woodsmoke, not the cold, not the way the old woman pressed bread on me, not the dog, not the silence after the bus had gone. The photograph shows roofs. The village was everything that happened between the roofs, and no camera has ever been built that can be pointed at that, and so I keep the photograph and distrust it, and keep the rest in my head.

subtopic: photographing and trying to capture a place
sentence: The light on the ruins in the late afternoon was the kind that makes a photographer greedy, and I took fifty pictures and then made myself stop, because the greed was getting between me and the place. I put the camera in the bag. I sat on a fallen column and watched the light move across the stones with no intention of capturing it, and the watching, free at last of the wish to keep, became a kind of communion.

subtopic: photographing and trying to capture a place
sentence: The child wanted to see herself on the screen and so I photographed her, and showed her, and she shrieked with delight and ran to fetch her friends, and the next ten minutes were a small joyful chaos of portraits, the camera no longer a barrier but a toy we all shared. Those photographs are blurred and badly lit and I would not trade them for anything, because they are the only ones I have where the place reached back and took part.

subtopic: photographing and trying to capture a place
sentence: I stopped photographing breakfast, sunsets, and my own feet somewhere in the second month, having understood that the camera, used so, was a way of not being present, a way of converting an experience into a chore. After that I photographed rarely and looked constantly, and the trip got larger, somehow, roomier, each day longer for being lived rather than documented, and I came home with few pictures and an enormous, unphotographable amount of having been there.

subtopic: photographing and trying to capture a place
sentence: The most beautiful thing I saw on the whole journey I did not photograph, because it lasted four seconds: a flock of birds turning all at once over a flooded field at dusk, the light catching their undersides, the whole flock flashing silver and then gone. There was no time for the camera and I am glad. The moment is mine, uncropped, unshareable, slightly fading, and entirely, perfectly, mine.

The children of the village adopted me within an hour of my arrival, a small delegation of them appearing at my guesthouse to inspect the foreigner, and thereafter I had an escort everywhere, a giggling fluctuating committee that walked me to the ruins, to the river, to the shop, narrating my journey to each other in a language I would never learn but somehow, by the end, almost understood.

A boy on the train practised his English on me for three hours, working through his entire vocabulary with a determination that was half ambition and half delight, and I corrected him gently and he corrected my pronunciation of his city's name, and we parted at his station the firmest of friends. He waved from the platform until the train took the curve. I hope he is somewhere now, speaking the English he was so fiercely building, sentence by sentence, on that long ride.

The children were curious about my hair, my camera, my strange shoes, my country, and they crowded close with a frank and friendly fearlessness, and I let them turn me over like an interesting object, because I was an interesting object, the first foreigner some of them had met. We had no shared words. We managed perfectly. A child and a stranger can build, out of gestures and laughter, a complete and joyful conversation.

A small girl sold me a single flower in the market with such gravity and such a good business sense that I bought three, and she counted my coins twice, and gave me a smile at the end of the transaction that was worth more than all the flowers. I carried them for the rest of the day, wilting, absurd, and could not bring myself to put them down, because they were the receipt of a meeting I did not want to be over.

The children played a game in the dust of the square that I could not understand and was not invited to join, and I sat on a step and watched it the way you watch any expert performance, the rules clearly intricate, the stakes clearly high, the players clearly the masters of a world that did not require me. There is a particular sweet exclusion in this, in watching the children of a foreign place be entirely, busily, themselves.

A boy attached himself to me as a guide, unasked, and led me through the medina with a confidence that brooked no argument, naming everything, demanding nothing, simply pleased to have a foreigner to be in charge of. At the gate I tried to pay him and he refused with dignity, having done it, he made clear, for the pleasure of the doing. I have been guided by professionals since and remember none of them as fondly as that small unpaid king of the lanes.

The schoolchildren on the road home in their neat uniforms found me hilarious, my height, my pack, my obvious lostness, and they fell in around me, a tide of small laughing escorts, and walked me to my destination by a route I am certain was not the shortest. They peeled off one by one as their own homes came up. The last two delivered me to my door, accepted my thanks with great seriousness, and ran off shrieking into the dusk.

A girl in the mountain village taught me, with infinite patience and visible despair at my slowness, the local way of counting on the fingers, and when at last I got it right she clapped, genuinely delighted by my small achievement. I have forgotten the counting. I have not forgotten the clap, the pure uncalculating pleasure of a child watching a clumsy adult finally manage a thing, and I have tried, since, to be that generous with my own delight.

The baby on the bus stared at me for an hour with the unblinking total attention that only babies and cats can manage, and I made the faces one makes, and at last it laughed, a sudden astonished sound, and its mother laughed, and the seats around us laughed, and the whole back of the bus was briefly bound together by the diplomacy of a foreign baby and a tired stranger pulling faces.

The children walked me to the edge of the village when I left, the way they had walked me everywhere, and stood in a clump on the road waving until the bus took the bend, and I waved back through the dusty window until I could not see them, and then a little after that. I have left many places. The leavings I find hardest are always the ones where the children come to the road, and wave, and do not understand why I cannot stay.

The border town had the particular character of all border towns, a place that faced two ways at once, where two currencies circulated and two languages mixed in the market and the cuisine was a negotiated peace between the kitchens of two countries. People here had relatives on both sides and crossed the line as casually as crossing a street. The town belonged, in the end, not to either nation but to the seam itself, and was the richer and stranger for it.

I spent two days in the frontier town waiting for a permit, and grew fond of its in-between quality, its shops full of the goods of both countries, its café where the talk slid between languages mid-sentence. The border was the town's whole reason for being and also its great inconvenience, and the townspeople regarded it with the weary affection one gives a difficult but profitable relative who is never, ever going to leave.

The town sat right against the line, and from its main square you could see the other country's hills, close enough to seem the same hills, which of course they were. The frontier ran through the landscape like a decision the landscape had never been consulted about. The town had learned to live astride it, to profit from it, to ignore it, and had become, in the process, a place that belonged fully to neither map and entirely to itself.

The market in the border town was the most interesting I saw in either country, because it was both countries at once, the goods, the smells, the haggling rhythms of two cultures crowded into one set of stalls. A trader sold me tea from one nation and dates from the other and gave me his prices in a third currency, the dollar, the lingua franca of all frontiers. The border, which divided so much, had at least built one excellent market.

The frontier town was full of people waiting, for permits, for relatives, for the right official to come on shift, and waiting had become its main industry, served by cheap hotels and patient cafés and men who knew, for a fee, how to make a wait shorter. I waited there myself, and joined the town's great patient population, and learned that a frontier is not a line but a wide blurred zone of delay, and the town was its capital.

The two halves of the divided town had once been one town, and you could still see it, the same architecture on both sides of the river that was now a border, the same family names, the same church spires built by the same vanished bishopric. History had cut the town in two with a line, and the line had hardened, and now each half was a foreign country to the other, close enough to wave across, and waving was, mostly, all that was allowed.

Smuggling was the frontier town's open secret and its quiet livelihood, and everyone knew the paths through the hills the customs posts did not watch, and the small profitable difference in the price of a litre of fuel from one side to the other. I do not think anyone here thought of it as crime. The border was an arbitrary inconvenience invented in a far capital; routing around it was simply common sense, a local skill, handed down.

The border town's hotels were full of truckers waiting for the customs to clear their loads, and the bar each night was a parliament of road weariness, drivers from a dozen countries trading routes and complaints and the names of officials to bribe and officials to fear. I sat among them, the only one not driving anything, and listened, and the frontier, in their telling, became a single enormous shared obstacle that the whole continent of trucks was forever, patiently, queuing to overcome.

The frontier town felt provisional, as if it had been built to be temporary and had simply, through the decades, forgotten to dismantle itself, the buildings cheap, the streets unfinished, the whole place leaning toward the crossing as toward an exit. Nobody seemed to be from here. Everyone was passing through, or had passed through and got stuck, and the town accommodated all of them with the loose informal hospitality of a permanent waiting room.

I liked the border town for the same reason I liked all border towns: it was a place with no fixed identity, and so it had been forced to become interesting, to make a culture out of mixture, a cuisine out of compromise, a daily life out of the constant low friction of the line. The capital cities of both countries were sure of themselves and therefore dull. The frontier town was sure of nothing, and therefore alive.

subtopic: night arrivals and the dark side of travel
sentence: I arrived in the city at two in the morning, the worst hour to arrive, when the buses have stopped and the hotels are dark and the only people on the street are the ones a tired traveller is taught to fear. I walked fast, pack tight, alert, until I found a lit doorway and a sleepy clerk and a room, and lay down still half on guard. Night arrivals strip travel of its romance and show you its other face, the wary, watchful, lonely one.

subtopic: night arrivals and the dark side of travel
sentence: The train was hours late and put me out in a strange town at midnight, and the romance of travel, which the daytime sustains so easily, drained completely away, and I was just a person far from home, tired, in the dark, in a place that owed me nothing. A taxi driver took pity, or took a fare, and got me to a bed. The town in daylight, the next morning, was charming. The town at midnight had been a different town entirely.

subtopic: night arrivals and the dark side of travel
sentence: There is a loneliness specific to travel, and it tends to come at night, in cheap rooms, when the day's distractions are spent and the foreignness presses in and there is no one, in this whole country, who knows your name. I have sat through it in a dozen rooms. It passes by morning, always, dissolved by light and coffee and the next day's road, but at night, in the dark, the road can feel less like freedom and more like exile.

subtopic: night arrivals and the dark side of travel
sentence: The bus broke down after dark on an empty road, and we sat in it, the headlights making a small lit world in all the country's blackness, and the romance of overland travel was nowhere to be found. A child cried. The driver swore under the engine. I watched the dark beyond the headlight pool and felt, honestly, afraid, and ashamed of being afraid, and understood that the bright traveller's tales never include enough of these dark patient frightened hours.

subtopic: night arrivals and the dark side of travel
sentence: I got lost after dark in a city I did not know, in a district I had been told to avoid, and the streets, charming by day, had become a maze with a different and colder logic, and every footstep behind me was a question. I do not romanticise this. It is the part of travel the brochures omit. I found my way out eventually, into light and people, and the relief was so total it was almost a happiness, but it was happiness built on fear.

subtopic: night arrivals and the dark side of travel
sentence: The night ferry docked at four in the morning and decanted us, the foot passengers, onto a black quay in a country we did not know, and we stood there in a confused tired cluster, no buses, no taxis, no plan, the romance of the sea crossing entirely behind us. Travel has these hours. They are not in the photographs. We waited for the dawn together, strangers, cold, and the dawn, when it came, returned us to being travellers rather than merely the stranded.

subtopic: night arrivals and the dark side of travel
sentence: Homesickness is a thing that ambushes you, and it ambushed me in a noisy bar in a happy city, surrounded by a celebration I had no part in, and for an hour I wanted nothing in the world but my own kitchen, my own language, the particular grey light of my own country. It passed. It always passes. But travel is not the unbroken delight the stories tell; it has these troughs, these sudden sharp wants, and an honest account must include them.

subtopic: night arrivals and the dark side of travel
sentence: I was robbed, mildly, in a city I will not name, a bag opened in a crowd, and the loss was small but the feeling was not, the sudden cold knowledge that the friendly anonymous crowd I had been moving through so trustingly contained, also, this. It changed the city for me, and I was sorry, because the city had done nothing, it was the same beautiful city, but I walked it differently after, and travel had shown me, again, its harder edge.

subtopic: night arrivals and the dark side of travel
sentence: The cheap hotel by the bus station had thin walls and a light that buzzed and a view of an air shaft, and I lay in it on a low night of the journey wondering, honestly, what I was doing, so far from everything, in this grim little room. Travel has these nights. The next day was glorious and I forgot the room entirely, but it had been real, and I keep it in the account, because a journey is the bad rooms too, not only the good ones.

subtopic: night arrivals and the dark side of travel
sentence: I reached the town after dark and could find nothing open, no food, no room, no welcome, only shuttered streets and the wind, and for an hour I walked them with a rising sense of having miscalculated, of having pushed the day too far. Then a light, a door, a woman who took me in. It ended well. But I have not forgotten that hour of dark uncertainty, and I think a traveller should not; it is the shadow that the bright days are bright against.

The island had one road, one shop, one boat a day to the mainland, and within a week I had begun to think of the boat's arrival as an event, a small daily drama on the quay. The island taught a slower arithmetic of time and need. You could not just pop out for a thing; you waited for the boat, or you did without, and there was a clean discipline in that, a return to an older relationship with distance.

The smallness of the island was its entire character: you could walk around it in a day, you knew every face by the second, and the sea was always there, at the end of every lane, reminding you of the exact dimensions of your temporary world. I came to love the confinement. An island is a place you can hold in your mind whole, all at once, and there is a peace in that completeness that the boundless mainland never gives.

When the storm cut the island off for three days, the islanders showed no concern at all, because being cut off was simply a thing islands did, a few times a year, and the island held everything it needed to wait one out. I waited it out with them. The shop's shelves thinned. The talk in the pub turned to other storms. And the island, sealed by the sea, became briefly the entire and self-sufficient world, which it had perhaps always secretly been.

The island's young people left, as island young people do, for the cities and the wider chances, and the island that remained was an island of the old and the returned, and a great tender melancholy lay over it like its frequent mist. I walked its emptying villages and its still-tended graveyards and felt the particular grief of a place that is loved and shrinking, held by fewer and fewer hands, beautiful and slowly going.

I took the boat to the small island simply because it was there, a low green shape on the horizon that the larger island ignored, and found on it forty people, a chapel, a beach of white sand, and a silence so complete I could hear my own blood. The boatman would come back for me at five. Between the leaving and the coming I had the island almost to myself, and I have rarely felt so far from everything, or so glad of it.

The islanders spoke a dialect the mainland found quaint and they found simply their language, and they kept festivals the mainland had forgotten, and they were proud and wary and kind in the particular layered way of people who have been, for centuries, slightly apart. The sea had preserved them, the way amber preserves things. I was a visitor to a place the modern world had reached late and lightly, and I trod carefully, and was grateful.

From the island the mainland was a blue line, an idea, a place where the buses ran and the choices multiplied, and after a week I noticed I had stopped looking at it. The island had become sufficient. Its single beach was beach enough; its one shop held all I had learned to want. The isolation that had felt, on the first day, like a limitation, had revealed itself, by the seventh, as a kind of wealth.

The lighthouse keeper's cottage was the last building on the island, and beyond it only rock and the long fall of the sea, and I walked out to it in the wind feeling I had reached an edge, a genuine end of things. The keeper was automated away years ago. The cottage stood empty, facing the weather. I sat in its lee and looked at the horizon, at all that water, and understood the island, finally, as a held breath between immensities.

The ferry to the island ran only in summer, and so the island had two completely different lives, the open thronged life of the warm months and the sealed private life of the winter, when the forty year-round residents had the place entirely to themselves. I visited in the shoulder season, the visitors gone, the winter not yet come, and the island in that pause felt like a stage between performances, swept, quiet, waiting, and very beautiful.

The island had been a place of exile once, a destination for the unwanted, and you could still feel it in the architecture of the old prison and in a certain inwardness of the light, and yet it was also, now, simply a place people loved and lived in. History and beauty lay on it in equal measure. I walked its cliffs in the clean wind and thought how a place can be both a punishment and a paradise, depending only on whether the sea is a wall or a road.

The vineyards covered the hills in long combed rows, following the contours with a patience that was itself a kind of architecture, and in the low autumn light each vine threw its own small shadow so the whole slope seemed corrugated with gold. The pickers worked along the rows, calling to each other, and the air was thick with the sweet bruised smell of the harvest, and I walked the lane between the vines feeling I had stepped into a landscape that had been composed.

The orchard in blossom was a single overwhelming fact, acre upon acre of it, white and pink and humming with bees, the trees so heavy with flower they seemed about to lift off, and the scent was a physical pressure. I lay down in the orchard grass and looked up through the blossom at the broken blue and thought that I had travelled a long way to see a number of famous things and that this, an ordinary orchard doing its annual ordinary miracle, was the most beautiful of all of them.

The rice terraces climbed the entire mountain in shining steps, each one a mirror of the sky, the work of forty generations of patient hands, and the scale of the labour, sustained across centuries, made me feel the deep difference between a landscape and a monument. This was both. I walked the narrow bunds between the flooded fields with the clouds moving in the water beneath me, an intruder in a cathedral the people here had farmed.

The olive groves were old, the trees gnarled into shapes that suggested great age and great suffering and great endurance, and some of them, the farmer told me, had been giving fruit since before the fall of empires. I put my hand on a trunk as wide as a doorway. The grove was quiet, silver-grey, the light coming through it soft and ancient, and I felt the particular awe of a landscape that had outlived everyone who had ever owned it and would outlive everyone who ever would.

The lavender ran to the horizon in violet bands, and the heat shimmered above it, and the smell, in the full sun, was almost too much, a sweetness with a sharpness at its centre. Bees worked the whole field at once, so that the air itself seemed to hum. I drove slowly through it with the windows down, in no hurry to reach the town, content simply to be passing, for these few kilometres, through a landscape that had decided to be beautiful for a living.

The fields had been worked into a quilt of different greens and golds, each parcel a different crop and a different family's labour, and from the hill above, the whole valley looked stitched, a piece of textile, the long collaboration of soil and weather and a thousand careful hands. A tractor crawled across one square of it. The pattern was not designed and was nonetheless a design, and I sat on the hill a long time, reading the valley as one reads a page.

It was the apple harvest, and the whole region smelled of it, and the orchards were full of ladders and the roads were full of trucks heaped with fruit, and the presses ran day and night turning the windfalls into a cider whose smell hung in every village. I stayed in a farmhouse at the centre of it all and was put, gently, to work, and learned that to be handed a task in a foreign place is one of the fastest routes there is into the heart of it.

The tea grew on the hill in waist-high rows of an intense and glossy green, and the pickers, mostly women, moved through it in bright clothes with baskets on their backs, their hands flickering over the bushes faster than I could follow. The hillside was beautiful and the work was hard and the two facts sat together uneasily in my mind. I bought a packet of the tea from the woman who had picked it, and have drunk it slowly, and thought of the hill each time.

The wheat was ready and the whole plateau was the colour of a lion, and the wind came across it in long visible waves, the field bending and rising like a single golden animal breathing. There was nothing else, no tree, no house, only the wheat and the wind and the enormous sky, and the road I was on ran through the middle of it dead straight to a horizon that the heat made tremble. I have seen mountains that moved me less.

The vineyard's owner walked me through the rows at dusk, naming the parcels, touching the leaves, telling me which slope caught the morning sun and which the afternoon, and his knowledge of his few hectares was deeper than my knowledge of any place I had ever lived. He had been reading this same small landscape for fifty years. The vines were his library. I left understanding that there is a kind of travel that goes not wide but down, and that he had been on it his whole life.

The music came out of a doorway as I passed, a stringed instrument I could not name and a voice doing something between singing and grieving, and I stopped in the street and listened until it ended, and then a little longer, in case there was more. There was not. But the music had given me the city in a way no sight had, had told me something about what this place felt, and I walked on carrying it, the soundtrack the place had handed me unasked.

In the mountain village the men sang after dinner, unaccompanied, a harmony so practised it sounded like one large voice, and the song was clearly old and clearly sad and clearly theirs, and I sat in the corner of the room not understanding a word and understanding everything. Music is the one language the traveller never needs translated. The song told me the village's whole history of hard winters and lost sons, and I have it still.

The bus driver played the same cassette for nine hours, a music I came, against my will and then with my whole heart, to love, and now whenever I hear those particular wailing strings and that particular drum I am back on that bus, the desert going by, the heat, the cracked seat, the entire long day. The music has become the place. I have bought the album since and it does not work at home; it needs the bus, the dust, the distance.

A wedding was happening somewhere in the town and the music of it carried over the rooftops half the night, a brass band and a great deal of percussion and, occasionally, a roar of collective joy, and I lay in my room not invited and not minding, borrowing the celebration through the window. The music told me the town knew how to be happy, knew it loudly and communally and well, and I fell asleep to the proof of it.

In the café an old man played an accordion, badly, to no one in particular, for the pleasure of it, and the café let him, and the music wove through the conversations and the coffee smell and the afternoon light as if it were a part of the furniture. It probably was. I drank two coffees I did not need just to stay for it, and the old man never looked up, playing, I think, mostly for himself, and generously letting the rest of us overhear.

The street musician at the metro entrance had a voice that stopped people, a real voice, sending some song up the tiled tunnel, and a crowd had gathered, the hurrying city briefly halted by beauty it had not budgeted for. I stood at the back and watched the faces, all of them softened, all of them caught, and thought that this was the city's true heart, not the monuments, but this: a stranger singing, and the strangers stopping to be moved.

I heard the call to prayer five times a day for a month and by the end I no longer heard it as exotic, or as anything but the city's own clock, the sound by which the day was jointed, and on the morning I left, very early, it rose in the dark from a dozen minarets at once, overlapping, and I stood with my bag waiting for the taxi and let the city sing me goodbye in the only voice it had been using all along.

The festival had drumming, and the drumming went on for hours, and it got into the body the way good drumming does, until the crowd was no longer listening to it but moving inside it, a single organism with one enormous pulse. I had not meant to dance and I was dancing. The drums had simply decided. There is a music that bypasses the mind entirely and speaks to something older, and on that hot night, in that crowd, I met it.

On the night train a man two compartments down played a flute, very softly, for perhaps twenty minutes, and the whole carriage went quiet to let him, and the music threaded out into the dark of the moving country and seemed to be playing the landscape itself. Then he stopped. No one spoke. The train rocked on. And I lay in my berth in the renewed silence feeling that I had been given something, and that the giver did not know it, and that this was the best way to be given things.

The children sang on the walk back from school, a round, the same few lines chasing each other down the road, and it was the most ordinary music imaginable and it undid me completely, because it was the sound of a place being entirely at home in itself, a place where the children sang on the way home as a matter of course. I followed a little way behind, listening, an eavesdropper on the simple happiness of somewhere I would shortly have to leave.

The storm came up the valley toward me with a visible front, a wall of grey dragging its rain like a curtain, and I watched it come from the dry side of the line and then it crossed the line and I was in it, drenched in seconds, laughing, because there is a particular exhilaration in being caught honestly out in weather, in having the sky simply happen to you with no roof in the argument.

The fog closed the road and the world at once, and I drove at the speed of caution through a whiteness that gave up a tree, a sign, a startled sheep, one at a time and then took them back, and the journey became a strange interior thing, the country reduced to the few yards the headlights could insist on. When the fog lifted, suddenly, on the high ground, the valley below was a lake of cloud, and I had been driving, it turned out, across the top of a sky.

The heat that day was a serious matter, a heat that bent the air over the road into liquid and emptied the towns and made every patch of shade a small contested territory, and travel slowed to the pace the heat permitted. I learned that day to respect the climate as the locals respected it, to stop when it said stop, to move when it relented, and the heat, treated so, became less an enemy and more a stern but predictable companion.

Snow began as I crossed the high ground, the first flakes almost playful and then, within the hour, serious, and the landscape simplified itself, lost its colour and its detail and became a country of white and the dark lines of walls, and the silence that snow brings came down with it. I walked through the muffled transformed world feeling I had been let into a secret, the secret of how a familiar landscape looks when the weather decides to start it over.

The monsoon, when it finally broke, broke completely, the sky simply opening, and the dusty waiting town turned in an hour to a town of running water and delighted children and the smell of wet earth that the whole country had been longing for. I stood under an awning and watched it, the rain so heavy it was a kind of weather you could not see through, and felt the collective relief of a place that had been holding its breath for months finally, gratefully, exhale.

The wind on the plateau was not weather but a presence, a constant pressure, a thing you leaned against and shouted over and were, after a few hours, exhausted by, and the few trees grew permanently bent, recording its direction. The people of the plateau had the wind's mark on them too, a squint, a hunch, a way of turning the face. I crossed it in a day and was glad to descend out of it, into the still air of the valley, where I could finally hear myself think.

The rain set in for a week, a soft grey persistent rain with no drama in it, and I stopped fighting it, bought a better coat, and discovered that the country in the rain was a different and quieter country, the colours deepened, the crowds thinned, the famous views softened into something more intimate. The rain had given me the place at half price and half population, and I came, by the week's end, to be almost sorry when the sun returned.

A thunderstorm caught me on the open hill and there was nowhere to go and so I simply sat it out, low against a rock, and watched the lightning walk the ridge opposite, magnificent and frightening, the thunder arriving a slow beat behind each flash. I have been told this was not wise. I do not regret it. The storm was the most powerful thing I have ever been close to, and to be small and exposed beneath it was a lesson I had needed in my exact size.

The frost that morning had silvered everything, every blade and twig and spider's web furred with white, and the cold was the clean still cold that comes only on a windless night, and the country I stepped out into was a country made overnight of glass and breath. The sun came up and began, slowly, to undo it. I walked fast to stay ahead of the thaw, wanting to keep the frozen world a little longer, and the world, indifferent, melted anyway, on schedule, into an ordinary bright day.

The heat haze made the whole road ahead a mirage, a shimmering pool that retreated as I approached, forever, and the distant mountains floated free of the earth, and the weather had turned the simple act of looking into something unreliable. I drove through the trembling unreal afternoon half-hypnotised. The desert in heat does not lie, exactly; it just shows you a version of itself that the cool of evening will quietly, completely, revise.

The man who showed me the ruins was not a guide by trade but a farmer whose land they stood on, and his telling of them was therefore not a script but a relationship, a lifetime of living beside the old stones, knowing which ones the sheep sheltered behind and where, as a boy, he had found a coin. The professional guides recite. He remembered. And to be shown a place by someone who simply knows it is the rarest and best of all guiding.

An old fisherman taught me, over an afternoon I had not planned, how to read the harbour, the signs in the water and the sky that told him what the next day would bring, and his knowledge was vast and entirely undocumented, the accumulated weather-lore of a life spent watching this one stretch of sea. I have forgotten most of it. But I remember the fact of it, that such knowledge exists, held in such people, learnable only by being there.

The woman at the loom let me sit and watch for as long as I liked, and as she worked she explained the patterns, what each one meant, which were for weddings and which for grief, and the cloth growing under her hands was revealed as a kind of writing, a language the village had woven for centuries. She did not charge me. She seemed glad to be asked. The best teachers I met on the road were almost never the ones whose job it was.

I hired a boy to guide me through the medina and got, for the small fee, not just directions but a whole apprenticeship in the place: which tea was good, which shop honest, which lane led where, the medina's working knowledge that no map carries. He delivered me, at the end, to my door, and to a far better understanding of the city, and I have thought since that I should have paid him a great deal more, for he had taught, not merely led.

The shepherd I fell into step with on the mountain track taught me, without meaning to, simply by answering my questions, the names of the plants, the use of each one, the way the season was read in the grass, and by the time our paths diverged the mountain had become, for me, a different and far richer place, legible where it had been merely scenic. He waved and went up; I went down, carrying his whole inadvertent lesson.

The monk who showed me the temple did it slowly, and in silence as much as in speech, and his guiding was really an invitation to a way of seeing, a pace, an attention. He would stop before a thing and simply wait until I had truly looked at it. I had been guided through temples before, briskly, informatively, and learned nothing. He guided me through one temple in two hours and I learned how to look, which is a thing you carry to every temple after.

An old man in the café, learning I was bound for the mountains, drew me a map on a napkin and annotated it with a lifetime's knowledge, the spring that was reliable and the one that was not, the farmer who would give a bed and the dog to be wary of. The napkin guided me for three days and was more use than the printed map in my pack. He had asked nothing. He had simply known the way, and could not bear to let a stranger go without it.

The cook let me into her kitchen, eventually, after I had eaten there enough times to be a fixture, and taught me the dish I had been ordering, her hands moving too fast, her instructions a stream of a language I had only fragments of, and yet I learned it, mostly by watching, the way such things are truly learned. I make it still. It is never as good. But the lesson was never really the dish; it was the kitchen, and the welcome, and the trust.

The taxi driver, hearing I had only one day in his city, appointed himself my guide, switched off the meter, and gave me his city instead of the tourist's, the bakery his mother used, the view his father had loved, the quiet square where he had courted his wife. It was the best tour I have had of anywhere. He charged me a fair flat fare at the end and refused a tip, having done it, he said, for the pleasure of showing off a place he loved.

The girl who taught me to count to ten in her language did it as a game, on a long bus ride, with great seriousness and frequent laughter at my failures, and she was perhaps nine, and she was, for those hours, entirely my teacher, and I her diligent and clumsy pupil. I have forgotten the numbers. I have not forgotten the lesson beneath the lesson: that to learn even a little of a place's language is to be handed a key, and that the youngest hands give the warmest keys.

The flight home crossed in a few hours a distance the journey out had taken weeks to build, and I watched the route unspool backward beneath the wing, the mountains, the coast, the sea, the whole hard-won geography compressed into an afternoon, and felt the particular vertigo of return, the way the going-out is a slow accumulation and the coming-back a sudden collapse. By dinner I would be home. The trip was already, impossibly, becoming a thing that had happened.

I had been gone long enough that home, when I reached it, had the faint strangeness of a place remembered rather than known, the rooms a little smaller, the light a little different, my own street briefly the street of a stranger. It passed within a day. Home reabsorbed me. But for that one day I saw my own life from the outside, with a traveller's eye, and what I saw was that it was, after all, and despite everything, a good place to have come back to.

The hardest part of the long journey was the last hour of it, the familiar road from the station, when the trip was over but not yet filed, and I sat on the local train among commuters who had not been anywhere and felt the enormous private weight of where I had been. They could not see it. It did not show. I carried the whole journey home invisibly, like a stone in a pocket, heavy and secret and mine.

I came home and for weeks the journey kept surfacing, a smell would do it, a slant of light, a word, and I would be back, briefly, completely, on some road, in some room, and then home would reassert itself. The trip did not end at the door. It went on ending for months, releasing itself slowly, and I let it, because the slow ending was, in its way, a continuation, the journey insisting on being remembered before it would consent to be over.

Returning to a place I had left changed is its own kind of travel, and I went back, years later, to the city that had been the start of everything, and it had moved on without me, as cities do, the café gone, the view built over, my own young self nowhere to be found in its streets. I had thought I was returning to a place. I was returning, it turned out, only to a memory of a place, and the city, the real one, owed me nothing, and gave me, gently, exactly that.

The journey home was down the same river I had come up, and the country reversed itself past the boat, the city to the suburbs to the farmland to the jungle, and I watched my whole route run backward and understood that I was not undoing the trip but completing it, closing the circle, and that a journey out and back is a different and more finished shape than a journey that only goes. The river delivered me to where I had begun, and I stepped off, complete.

I had been away so long that I had to relearn my own kitchen, the trick of the tap, the cupboard the cups lived in, and there was something both sad and instructive in that, in being briefly a tourist in my own life. The skills of travel had crowded out the skills of home. They came back. But I have kept, ever since, a small useful awareness that home, too, is a place, and could in principle be visited, and looked at, with fresh and grateful eyes.

The last night before flying home I walked the city I was leaving for hours, trying to fix it, to take a final reading, knowing that this was the last time I would see these particular streets as a person who lived in them, however briefly, rather than as a person who had once passed through. The city did not know it was being farewelled. It went about its evening. And I walked it, memorising, the way you memorise a face at a station.

Coming home, I found that the trip had quietly recalibrated me, that things which had loomed large before I left now seemed small, and small things now seemed precious, and that the journey had functioned, without my noticing, as a long slow correction of perspective. This is the real souvenir, the one that cannot be packed: not the photographs, not the trinkets, but the altered sense of proportion, the traveller's gift, carried home invisibly inside the returning traveller.

I reached my own front door at last and stood a moment before opening it, the pack heavy, the journey behind me entire, and felt the strange double thing that all returns contain: the deep animal gladness of being home, and the immediate, quiet, already-stirring wish to be, once more, somewhere else. The door opened. Home took me back. And the wish settled down to wait, as it always does, patient, certain of its eventual turn.

The tundra went to the horizon in every direction, flat and treeless and immense, a green-brown plain stretching under a sky that took up most of the world, and the scale of it was a thing the body registered before the mind, a sense of having walked out into a room with no walls. A bird called somewhere. The wind moved the low plants. And I stood in the middle of all that openness feeling, not lost exactly, but profoundly, usefully, small.

The sun did not set, and so the days lost their joints, and I found myself walking at what should have been midnight in a light like late afternoon, the whole north awake around me, birds singing, the land glowing. The body rebelled at first and then surrendered. Time, up here in the summer, was a suggestion. I slept when tired, walked when not, and lived for a while in a single enormous day that the calendar insisted, against all evidence, was several.

We crossed the frozen river on a road that was simply the ice itself, marked with poles, and the strangeness of driving on water, of the river beneath us holding the weight of the truck in its winter discipline, never quite stopped feeling like a transgression.
