The ice creaked and boomed, settling, doing whatever ice does. The driver was unconcerned. The river would be a road until spring, and then, with no fuss, it would be a river again.

The cold in the far north was not a temperature but an environment, a thing you dressed for as you might dress for the sea, with respect and the right equipment, and outside that equipment it would, simply and impersonally, kill you. I learned to move within its rules. And within them the frozen country was beautiful beyond anything, the light low and gold and pink for hours, the snow blue in the shadows, the air so cold it sparkled with its own frozen breath.

The aurora came out while we waited for it in the cold, a curtain of green light that rippled and reached and folded across the whole northern sky, silent, slow, indifferent, and the small group of us stood with our heads back making the involuntary sounds people make. I had crossed half the world to see it and it owed me nothing and it gave me everything, and then, after an hour, it faded, and we went in, changed, to the stove and the dark.

The northern village was small and tough and turned inward against the long dark, and in the deep of the winter, the locals told me, the sun did not rise at all for weeks, and the village lived by lamplight and by each other, and waited. I visited in the brief bright summer. But I could feel the winter in the architecture, in the stacked firewood, in a certain readiness, and I admired, deeply, the stubbornness of a people who had chosen to live where the year itself goes dark.

We travelled by sled behind dogs that wanted nothing in the world but to run, and the only sounds were the hiss of the runners and the dogs' breathing and the enormous silence of the frozen forest pressing in on both sides. The cold streamed past. The white country unrolled. I had thought this would feel like an activity and it felt instead like a kind of prayer, fast and silent and clean, the old way of crossing the snow, and the dogs and the snow and I were briefly one moving thing.

The glacier was a frozen river that moved a few inches a year, and walking on it I could hear it, the deep groans and sudden cracks of all that ice in its century-slow descent, and the meltwater ran in blue veins across its surface and vanished, roaring, down shafts to its hidden underside. It was the most alive-seeming dead thing I have stood on. I felt, on the glacier, the planet's geological pulse, slow and vast and entirely uninterested in the brief warm creature it carried.

The pack ice stretched from the ship's bow to the horizon, a broken white country, and the vessel pushed into it with a sound of grinding and a steady patient violence, the floes splitting and tilting and sliding under, and a seal watched us pass with mild dark eyes from a slab of its own front garden. There was no land. There was only the ice, and the ship's slow argument with it, and the cold clean light, and I stood at the rail for hours, unable to go in, unwilling to miss a yard of it.

The northern light in winter was a long blue twilight that served as both dawn and dusk, the sun never quite arriving, the day a single extended hesitation between dark and dark, and it should have been depressing and was instead, somehow, beautiful, a country lit like the inside of a sapphire. The villagers had made their peace with it. They lit their windows gold against the blue, and the gold and the blue together, seen from the cold road, were the colours of a kind of stubborn human hope.

We had no shared language and a great deal to say, the old man and I, and so we said it in the other way, with hands and faces and drawn pictures and the few words each of us had stolen from the other's tongue, and the conversation, slow and inventive and frequently hilarious, lasted the whole train journey. I learned about his sons. He learned about my country's weather. We understood, I think, most of it, and the rest we forgave.

The woman spoke not a word I knew and yet over the meal she made it entirely clear that I was too thin, that I should eat more, that my journey was foolish and my mother must worry, and all of this came across with perfect clarity through tone and gesture and the universal grammar of a concerned older woman. Language, I have learned, is only the top layer of communication. Beneath it people are remarkably, reliably, legible.

I carried a phrasebook and used it badly, and my mispronunciations were a source of great and kindly entertainment everywhere I went, and I came to understand that the mistakes were not a barrier but a bridge, that to mangle a few words of a person's language is to hand them a small gift of laughter and to declare, clumsily but unmistakably, that you have at least tried, that you have come not to demand but to meet.

The two of us communicated entirely through a third language, neither of ours, a few hundred words of trade-route English that we both held imperfectly, and there was something fitting in that, two strangers meeting on the neutral ground of a borrowed tongue. We discussed prices, then politics, then, haltingly, our lives. The borrowed language was just enough. It is astonishing, I have found, how little language two willing people actually need.

A teenager was deputised to translate, as teenagers always are, and she rendered the conversation between me and her grandmother with a visible effort and frequent giggles, and a good deal, I am sure, was lost or improved in the passage. But the grandmother's warmth came through untranslated, as warmth does, and the teenager's pride in her school English came through too, and the whole three-way exchange was clumsy and slow and one of the warmest of the trip.

The shopkeeper and I conducted our entire negotiation through a calculator, passed back and forth, the numbers our only shared language, and it was a perfectly complete conversation in its way, an offer, a counter, a feigned outrage, a final grudging smile, all of it expressed in glowing digits and eyebrows. I overpaid, certainly. I did not mind. The calculator-conversation had been worth the margin, a small wordless theatre we had staged together.

On the long walk we fell silent, the local man and I, because we had exhausted our tiny shared vocabulary in the first hour, and the silence that followed was not awkward but companionable, two people walking the same road, content to point things out, to share food, to be wordlessly together. I have had emptier conversations in my own language. The walk taught me that company does not, in the end, require talk; it requires only presence, and goodwill, and a shared direction.

I learned ten words of the language and deployed them constantly and probably wrongly, hello and thank you and beautiful and where, and these ten words, scattered through every transaction, transformed my reception entirely, and I understood that the words were not really for communication but for courtesy, a way of saying I see that this is your country and your tongue and I have not simply expected you to accommodate mine.

The old farmer wanted, very much, to tell me something, and lacking any shared word he took me by the arm and walked me to it, to a view, to a tree, to a particular spot, and showed me with his whole body what his mouth could not say, and I understood: this was his place, and he loved it, and he wanted, before I left, for me to know that. I knew it. Some things are better said by being walked to than by being spoken.

We laughed a great deal, the family and I, mostly at the language itself, at my attempts and their attempts and the wonderful failures in between, and the laughter became the real conversation, the thing we were actually doing, and by the end of the evening we were friends in the way that people who have laughed together are friends, having communicated, through all the broken words, the one thing that matters most, which is simple goodwill.

Travelling alone, I learned the particular texture of my own company, the long unbroken hours of it, and discovered that I was, mostly, decent company, that the mind left to itself on a quiet road does not panic but settles, turns things over, grows calm. There were lonely hours, certainly. But there were more hours of a clean self-sufficient quiet, and I came home knowing myself a little better, which is, perhaps, the secret real purpose of going alone.

The solitary traveller is more available, I found, more porous, more easily fallen into conversation with, because a person alone is a kind of open door, and so my solo journey was paradoxically full of company, of strangers who would never have approached a couple or a group. Alone, I was approachable. Alone, I belonged to no party and could therefore briefly join any. The solitude was not isolation; it was a doorway, and people kept walking through it.

There is a freedom to travelling alone that I had underestimated until I had it: every decision mine, the pace mine, the route mine, the day shaped by no negotiation but my own changing whim. I could stop for an hour to watch a river. I could change the plan entirely over breakfast. The solitude was, in this sense, a luxury, a rare and total ownership of my own time, and I spent it greedily, and well.

The loneliness, when it came, came in the evenings, at the table for one, watching the families and the couples and the easy groups, and I would not pretend it did not. But I learned to let it pass through me rather than fight it, to treat it as weather, and it always passed, and the morning always restored me. The solo road has these dusks. They are the price, and it is not, in the end, a high one.

Alone on the mountain, miles from anyone, I felt the solitude reach a kind of purity, a silence with no human edge to it at all, and instead of the fear I had half expected there came a great calm, a sense of being exactly the right size, a small warm creature on a large indifferent slope. I have chased that feeling since. It is hard to find in company. It needs the genuine solitude, the real absence of other people, to come.

I talked to myself on the long empty roads, out loud, narrating, arguing, and was not ashamed of it, because the solitary traveller develops these habits and they are harmless and they keep the mind limber. I had whole conversations with the absent. I planned, I remembered, I rehearsed. The road alone is a long thinking, and I came off it with my mind, somehow, tidier, sorted, a number of old questions quietly resolved by all that walking and muttering.

Travelling alone, every small triumph was wholly mine, the found room, the crossed border, the meal successfully ordered, and there was a clean private satisfaction in that, an unsharable but real pride in having managed, in a strange place, entirely on my own resources. I had not known I could. The solo journey teaches you this above all: the discovery, slow and sturdy, that you are more capable, more durable, more resourceful than your settled life had ever required you to find out.

The solitude sharpened my attention, I noticed, because there was no companion to dilute the looking, no conversation to pull my eyes from the window, and so I saw more, alone, saw the place with a clearer and greedier eye. A shared journey is warmer. A solo journey is sharper. I have done both and valued both, but for the pure act of seeing a place, of taking it in entire, I have come to prefer the keen lonely clarity of going by myself.

There were days on the solo road when I spoke to no one at all, when the whole day passed in silence, and I learned that such days were not empty but spacious, that the mind, ungoverned by talk, found its own slow rhythms, and that an unbroken silent day, far from being a thing to dread, was a thing to be quietly grateful for, a rare unhurried room in which to simply, fully, be.

I went alone because I wanted the journey unmediated, the place itself and not a place filtered through a companion's running commentary, and I got what I wanted: a long solitary intimacy with the road, an undiluted dose of the world. It was sometimes hard. It was never, not for one hour, regretted. And I came home certain that everyone should, once, go somewhere far entirely alone, and meet, on the empty road, the person they turn out to be.

sentence: In the middle of the desert, miles from any town, I came upon a single telephone box, painted red, perfectly maintained, standing alone in all that sand with its door slightly ajar, and there was no explanation, and no one to ask, and I have never found one. The road delivers these things. The strange does not announce itself; it simply stands there, in the sand, beside the highway, declining utterly to make sense.

sentence: The town we passed through was holding, for reasons no one could or would explain, a festival entirely devoted to a particular vegetable, and the streets were hung with effigies of it, and a parade went by carrying an enormous model of it, and the whole population seemed sincerely, joyfully invested. I did not understand it. I did not need to. The road shows you these private local strangenesses and asks only that you witness them and move on.

sentence: I woke on the night bus to find that we had stopped, in the dark, in a place that was simply a vast field of parked buses, hundreds of them, engines off, lights off, and no people anywhere, a silent fleet asleep in the middle of nowhere, and then we moved on, and I have never known what it was. The road has a dream logic at night. It assembles these tableaux, shows them to the half-asleep traveller, and dismantles them before morning.

sentence: The hotel had a corridor that, the more I walked it, seemed not to end where the building's exterior said it should, and I never resolved this, and I have decided not to want to. Travel loosens the joints of the ordinary. In a strange building, in a strange town, in a country whose rules I only half knew, a slightly impossible corridor seemed no stranger than anything else, and I stopped, after the second night, even thinking about it.

subtopic: the strange and the surreal on the road
sentence: A man on the train was travelling, he explained at length and with great seriousness, with a suitcase that contained, he said, the wind, and he would not open it, lest the wind escape, and he asked me to keep my voice down near it. I kept my voice down. The road is full of these gentle private madnesses, and the kind thing, the traveller's thing, is simply to accept the terms, to lower the voice, to let the man and his suitcase travel undisturbed.

subtopic: the strange and the surreal on the road
sentence: We drove for an hour past a procession of statues, life-sized, concrete, placed at intervals along the empty highway, figures in old-fashioned clothes frozen mid-gesture, and there was no sign, no town, no apparent maker, just the statues, watching the road. The driver shrugged when I asked. The road has these long inexplicable installations. Someone made them, for some reason, and then the reason left, and the statues stayed, gesturing at the traffic forever.

subtopic: the strange and the surreal on the road
sentence: In the museum of the small town, among the ordinary local artefacts, there was one glass case containing a single shoe and a handwritten card that said only its date, and nothing else, no name, no story, and the caretaker, when I asked, looked at it as if seeing it for the first time and could tell me nothing. The road keeps these orphaned facts. A shoe, a date, and a silence, displayed with care, meaning something once, to someone, now lost.

subtopic: the strange and the surreal on the road
sentence: The village clock struck thirteen, distinctly, and no one in the square so much as looked up, and when I mentioned it the café owner said yes, it had always done that, the thirteenth strike, and that was simply the clock, and the village had long ago stopped finding it remarkable. I found it remarkable for both of us. The road shows you a place's strangeness fresh, the strangeness its own inhabitants have worn smooth with familiarity and ceased to see.

subtopic: the strange and the surreal on the road
sentence: I asked directions and was sent, with great confidence and apparent goodwill, in what turned out to be precisely the wrong direction, and this happened so consistently, in that one region, that I began to suspect a courtesy I did not understand, a custom in which the giving of directions mattered more than their accuracy. I never confirmed it. The road leaves you with these unsolved small anthropologies, these customs glimpsed and never quite decoded.

subtopic: the strange and the surreal on the road
sentence: At the crossroads in the middle of the plain there was a hotel, a large grand hotel, with a doorman and lit windows and the sound of a piano, and no town for fifty miles in any direction, and no road but the one I was on, and I did not stop, and I have wondered ever since whether I should have. The road offers these doors. It sets them in the emptiness and lights them and leaves it entirely to you whether to find out what is inside.

The old quarter was a knot of lanes too narrow for cars, and so it had kept the pace of an earlier century, the pace of feet, and walking it I felt the city slow around me, the centuries thinning, the modern town's noise filtering down to almost nothing. Washing hung between the upper floors. A cobbler worked in a doorway. The quarter was not preserved, exactly; it was simply still being used, the same way, by the same kind of life, and that was its quiet astonishment.

I lost a whole morning in the old quarter, deliberately, following its logic, which was the logic of accumulation rather than design, lanes that had grown rather than been planned, opening without warning onto a tiny square, a workshop, a shrine. The quarter had no centre and no grid. It had only itself, dense and folded and ancient, and to walk it was to read a city that had been written, slowly, by everyone who had ever lived in it.

The old neighbourhood was where the city kept its memory, the only district the developers had not yet reached, and you could see, in its crooked streets and its sagging beautiful houses, what the whole city had once been before it grew rich and tall and forgot. The locals were proud and slightly defensive of it. I understood why. They were the keepers of the city's older self, and the keeping was getting harder, and the quarter, lovely and outnumbered, knew it.

In the historic quarter the trades still clustered by lane, the metalworkers here, the dyers there, the carpenters in their own loud street, an arrangement that the rest of the city had abandoned centuries ago, and walking through it was walking through a living diagram of how a city used to organise itself. The hammering, the smells, the apprentices: it was not a museum. It was a working district, doing now what it had done forever, and meaning to keep on.

The old quarter came alive at dusk, when the day's heat let go and the residents brought their chairs out onto the cooling stones, and the lanes filled with the low pleasant noise of a neighbourhood that knew itself, the children, the gossip, the smell of a hundred kitchens. I sat on a step at the edge of it. No one minded. The quarter had been absorbing strangers for a thousand years and could easily absorb one more, for an evening, on a step.

The houses of the old quarter leaned toward each other across the lanes until their upper floors nearly touched, and the sky was reduced to a bright crooked ribbon overhead, and the light came down filtered, golden, the way light comes into a forest. The quarter had grown like a forest too, slowly, organically, each house finding its space among the others. I walked its dim warm canyons and felt the city's great age settle around me like a coat.

I found a café in the old quarter that had been a café for two hundred years, and the proof was on the walls, the photographs and the smoke-darkening and the worn particular shine of the marble counter, and I drank a coffee there feeling the long company of everyone who had drunk one before me. The quarter was full of such places, doing the same thing they had always done, in the same room, and the continuity of it was a comfort I had not known I needed.

The old quarter was being slowly hollowed out, the residents priced away, the houses turned to lodgings for visitors like me, and I felt, walking it, the particular guilt of the traveller, the awareness that my very presence was part of the pressure changing the place I had come to love. The quarter was still beautiful. But it was emptying of the life that had made it, and I trod it carefully, and tipped well, and knew it was not enough.

Behind a plain door in the old quarter was a courtyard, and in the courtyard a tree older than the country's current borders, and an old woman who let me sit beneath it because I had admired it, and we sat there, in the green hidden quiet, while the city roared on, unsuspected, a few feet away. The old quarter is full of these concealments. It hides its best things behind plain doors, and gives them only to those who ask, and look, and are still.

The wall of the old quarter still stood, mostly, ringing the ancient heart of the city, and walking its top I could see the two cities at once, the old one folded small and dense within the ring, the new one sprawling beyond it to the haze. The wall had once been the whole boundary of the known and the safe. Now it was a walkway, a viewpoint, a memory. But it still held the old quarter in its arms, and the old quarter still, somehow, felt held.

The river was so wide that the ferry crossing took most of an hour, and standing at the rail I watched one bank sink and the other slowly rise, and for a long stretch in the middle there was only water, the great brown body of the river going about its enormous business, carrying the country's soil to the sea. A river that wide is not a thing you cross so much as a thing you are briefly granted passage over, and I felt the grant, and was grateful.

The delta was a country still being made, the river dropping its load of mountains here at the sea's edge, building new land, drowning old, and the people who lived on it had learned to live with that uncertainty, to build light, to move, to treat the ground itself as a kind of slow tide. I travelled it by boat, because there was no other honest way, and the delta unrolled, half land and half water and entirely alive, and refused, gloriously, to hold still.

We crossed the river at a town that existed only because the river had to be crossed somewhere, a town of ferries and waiting and the trades that grow around a chokepoint, and the river there was a wide grey fact that organised everything. I waited my turn with the trucks and the bicycles and the patient crowd, and when the ferry came we all went down to it together, and the river took us, indifferent, to the far and identical bank.

The river was the country's main street, and everything happened on it or beside it: the markets, the temples, the funerals, the laundry, the children's whole summer. I travelled down it for days and the river never stopped being the centre of the view and the centre of the life. The land was just the river's banks. The road was just the river's spare. The river was the place itself, moving, and the country had simply arranged itself along its length.

At the river's mouth the fresh water and the sea met in a wide zone of confusion, the colours blending, the river's brown slowly conceding to the sea's grey-green, and the boats of two different worlds, the river boats and the sea boats, mingled there, in the meeting place. I crossed that zone in a vessel that belonged to neither, and felt the water change beneath the hull, and understood that I was at a true edge, where a river finished being a river and a sea began.

The flood had come, as it came every year, and the river had spread itself across the whole delta, and the villages stood up out of the brown water on their stilts and their raised mounds, islanded, connected now only by boat, and the people went about their flooded lives with the calm of long practice. I travelled among them by boat and saw that the flood was not a disaster here but a season, expected, even needed, the river simply doing the thing the delta had been shaped by it to do.

The bridge across the great river was a long time in the crossing, and from its centre I could see the river curving away in both directions, vast and patient and old, dividing the country into a left bank and a right bank that had, the locals insisted, quite different characters. I crossed from one to the other and could not, honestly, tell the difference, but I believed them, because a river that great surely does divide more than the land.

The river in flood season carried whole trees, and rafts of vegetation, and once, the boatman said, a house, the river simply taking what it wanted from upstream and carrying it down, and we threaded our boat through this slow brown traffic of debris with a care that the boatman made look like ease. The river was powerful and unsentimental. It built the delta and it took the delta back, and the people on it had learned to ask of it only passage, and to expect nothing else.

I reached the river at dusk and the crossing was the last ferry, and the boat went over the wide darkening water with its lights on, and the far bank was a low line of answering lights, and the river between was black and enormous and entirely silent. The crossing felt, in the dark, like more than a crossing, like a passage between two conditions, and I stood at the rail in the river-cool air feeling the day end exactly in the middle of all that moving water.

The delta had a thousand channels and the boatwoman knew them as a city-dweller knows streets, and we went down avenues of water between walls of green, past floating houses and floating shops and a floating school, and I understood that here the boundary between the river and the land had never really been drawn, that the people had simply, sensibly, decided to be amphibious, and had built a whole working civilisation on that decision.

subtopic: capitals and their grand public spaces
sentence: The great square at the heart of the capital was built to make the individual feel small, and it succeeded, and I stood in the middle of all that deliberate vastness, the monumental facades on every side, the immense paved emptiness, feeling the particular thing such spaces are designed to make you feel: that the state is large and old and will outlast you. It was an effective argument. It was also, in the low evening light, undeniably beautiful, and I gave it both responses at once.

subtopic: capitals and their grand public spaces
sentence: The capital's grand avenue ran straight as a ruler from the palace to the monument, a kilometre of imperial intention, and walking it I felt the city's whole self-image, its wish to be permanent and important and impressive. The avenue delivered the wish. But at its edges, in the side streets, the real city carried on, smaller and warmer and more honest, and I found, as I always find in capitals, that I preferred the side streets, and forgave the avenue its grandeur.

subtopic: capitals and their grand public spaces
sentence: The plaza filled, each evening, with the whole life of the capital, the families and the lovers and the vendors and the old men, and the grand official space designed for parades and proclamations was quietly, daily, repurposed by the citizens into something better, a living room, a stage for the small ordinary theatre of a population at leisure. I sat on the steps of a monument to a forgotten general and watched the city do this, take its solemn square and make it kind.

subtopic: capitals and their grand public spaces
sentence: The capital had built itself a centre of marble and bronze, of squares and ministries and a cathedral of a railway station, all of it announcing the nation to itself and to its visitors, and I walked it dutifully and was duly impressed and slightly oppressed. Then I turned a corner and found a market, loud and cheap and entirely unmonumental, and felt the relief of it, the city remembering, in that one street, that it was also just a place where people lived and bought their onions.

subtopic: capitals and their grand public spaces
sentence: The grand boulevard had been laid out by an emperor who wanted his capital to rival the great cities of the world, and it did, and the trees were enormous and the buildings were palaces and the whole long perspective was a triumph of will and money and a certain ruthless vision. I admired it. I also thought of the old crowded quarter the boulevard had been cut through to make, the lanes and the lives erased to clear this magnificent line, and the admiration cooled, a little, as it should.

subtopic: capitals and their grand public spaces
sentence: The capital's central park was the lung the dense city breathed through, and on a warm afternoon the whole population seemed to be in it, lying on the grass, rowing the lake, walking the long designed avenues of trees, and the park, which an old regime had built as a pleasure ground for the few, now belonged, unanswerably, to everyone. I lay on the democratic grass among them and felt the city, in the park, at its happiest and most itself.

subtopic: capitals and their grand public spaces
sentence: The square in front of the parliament was where the capital came to argue with itself, and there was a protest the day I passed through, orderly and loud, the citizens using the grand official space for the purpose a grand official space is, in the end, most honourably used for. The monuments looked on. The state's stone faces watched the state's living people shout at them. It was, I thought, exactly what such a square is for, and the city seemed healthier for the noise.

subtopic: capitals and their grand public spaces
sentence: The capital's main square was older than the nation, had been a market and a place of execution and a parade ground and now was simply a square, ringed with cafés, crossed by everyone, and all its histories lay in it together, invisible, underfoot. I drank a coffee at its edge and watched the tourists photograph the facades and the locals cut across without a glance, and felt the strange depth of a public space that had been continuously, variously public for a thousand years.

subtopic: capitals and their grand public spaces
sentence: At night the capital lit its monuments, and the grand square became a stage set, the floodlit columns and domes and the great equestrian statue all glowing against the dark, and the effect was theatrical and beautiful and slightly unreal. The daytime square was a thoroughfare; the night square was a spectacle. I crossed it slowly, the only one not hurrying, taking the free show the city put on for itself every single night, whether anyone watched or not.

subtopic: capitals and their grand public spaces
sentence: The capital's ceremonial heart was vast and gleaming and a little cold, and I did the circuit of it, the palace, the cathedral, the tomb of the unknown soldier with its small eternal flame, and felt, as one is meant to feel, the weight of the nation's idea of itself. Then I walked out of the grand district and into an ordinary one, and bought a pastry, and the capital became, again, a city, and I liked it much better for being, also, just that.

The town was in no guidebook and had no reason to be, no monument, no famous view, no celebrated dish, and I had stopped there only because the bus had, and I had two hours, and so I walked it, and found exactly what such towns always offer: an ordinary place being ordinarily itself, a square, a church, a café, a life. There is a particular pleasure in the unfamous town. It performs for no one. It simply is, and lets you, for two hours, simply be there.

I have made a habit of stopping in the towns the guidebooks skip, the ones marked, if at all, with the smallest dot, because they hold the country's ordinary truth, the life as it is actually lived between the famous places. This one had a hardware shop, a war memorial, a river, a cat asleep in a window, and an old man who said good morning to me as if I belonged there. The famous towns dazzle. The skipped towns, quietly, befriend.

The town the guidebook ignored gave me the best afternoon of the trip, precisely because nothing was expected of me there, no sight to be ticked, no view to be admired, and so I simply sat in its square and watched its small commerce and its slow conversations and its children, and the town, asking nothing, gave everything: a clear unhurried look at the actual country, the country as it is when no one is looking, which is to say, when only I was.

Every famous town was once an unfamous one, and I like to think of the skipped towns I pass through as places merely waiting, or, better, places that have wisely declined the dubious promotion, that have kept their square uncrowded and their café for the locals and their pace their own. This one had clearly so declined. It went about its modest business with a self-possession the famous towns have lost, and I envied it, a little, its happy obscurity.

The small town had one of everything, one church, one school, one bar, one shop, one bus a day, and the economy of it, the lack of all surplus and choice, was itself a kind of clarity. Life here was not a menu. It was a given. I walked the single main street in twenty minutes and then walked it again, slower, and the town, which the guidebook had not mentioned, taught me more about the region than the region's celebrated capital had managed in three days.

I asked the café owner in the unfamous town whether tourists ever came, and she thought about it and said, sometimes, lost ones, like me, and we both laughed, and she gave me an extra pastry for being a lost one. The town was not on the way to anywhere. You did not pass through it; you had to mean it, or, like me, mistake it. And it rewarded the mistake with a kindness the towns on the main routes had long ago run out of.

The town had a museum, one room, run by a volunteer, full of the small local past, the old photographs and the farm tools and the relics of a vanished industry, and the volunteer walked me through it with a pride that the great national museums, for all their treasures, never quite manage. This was his town's memory, kept by his own hands. I have forgotten what great museums showed me. I remember that one room, and the man, and the care.

The skipped town sat in a landscape the guidebooks did praise, and so the travellers passed it at speed on their way to the praised landscape, and never knew that the town itself, small and plain, was the better thing, the warmer thing, the place where the landscape's people actually lived. I stopped. I always stop. And the town gave me, for the price of a missed connection, an afternoon of the real country that the praised landscape, beautiful and crowded, could not.

There was nothing to do in the small town and so I did nothing, expertly, for a whole afternoon: sat, watched, drank coffee, watched, walked the river, watched. The town did not mind. It had no expectations to disappoint. And in the doing of nothing, in the long unstructured hours of it, the town slowly revealed itself, the way a quiet person does, and by evening I knew it, and liked it, and was sorry, genuinely sorry, that the morning bus would take me on.

The guidebook gave the region forty pages and the town not one line, and yet the town had a square as fine as any, and a baker as good, and a light in the late afternoon that lay along its single street like a blessing, and I sat in that light thinking that the guidebook's silence was, in a way, the town's good fortune, the thing that had kept it itself. Some places are best served by being left off the map, and this, I thought, was one.

subtopic: the food of a place and what it reveals
sentence: I have come to believe that you cannot know a place until you have eaten its everyday food, not the restaurant version but the home version, the thing the grandmother makes on a Tuesday, and in this country a family let me into that, into a meal of beans and bread and a green herb sauce, and I understood the region better from that one table than from a week of its sights. The food told me what the land gave, what the people valued, how they gathered. It told me, in short, the place.

subtopic: the food of a place and what it reveals
sentence: The dish was simple, a few ingredients, and yet it carried the whole logic of the region in it: the spice that the old trade routes had brought, the grain that the dry hills would grow, the preserving technique that the long winters had demanded. To eat it was to taste a history. I have stopped, in my travels, ordering the elaborate things; the simple local dish, properly understood, is the deeper text, and I read it now, slowly, everywhere I go.

subtopic: the food of a place and what it reveals
sentence: The market told me what the season was before the calendar did, the stalls heaped with whatever the land was giving that week, and the local cooking simply followed, obedient, seasonal, and I ate, that month, what the place itself was eating, what it had to eat. There is an honesty in that I had lost at home, where every month tastes the same. The place's food was tied to the place's year, and eating it tied me, briefly, to both.

subtopic: the food of a place and what it reveals
sentence: The way the meal was served told me as much as the meal: the shared central dishes, the absence of individual plates, the expectation that you would reach in, that eating was a collective act, not a private one. I learned the etiquette by watching and by gentle correction. And I understood that the food was not just food here; it was a daily lesson in how the culture believed people should be together, and I was, for the length of the meal, enrolled.

subtopic: the food of a place and what it reveals
sentence: I asked an old woman why the local bread was shaped the way it was, and her answer ran back through the oven it was baked in, the wood that fired the oven, the trees that the hills grew, the whole landscape contained in the curve of a loaf. Food, asked the right questions, opens like that. The bread was not just bread. It was the region, kneaded, and I ate the rest of my piece with a new and careful attention.

subtopic: the food of a place and what it reveals
sentence: The festival food was different from the everyday food, richer, rarer, the dishes that the year had been saving up for, and to be in the town on the feast day was to taste what the place considered a treat, a celebration, a splurge, and that told me something tender about it, about its idea of joy. The everyday food shows you a place's character. The festival food shows you its dreams, and I ate the town's dreams, that day, and they were sweet, and fried, and shared.

subtopic: the food of a place and what it reveals
sentence: The cheese of that valley existed nowhere else, could exist nowhere else, because it was made of that valley's particular grass and that valley's particular weather and that valley's particular slow inherited method, and to eat it was to eat the valley itself, distilled. I bought a wedge from the farm that made it. The cheesemaker did not think of his cheese as remarkable. It was simply the taste of home, and he had given me, in a paper wrapping, a piece of his.

subtopic: the food of a place and what it reveals
sentence: The poorest region I passed through had the most inventive food, because invention is what scarcity teaches, and the dishes there did extraordinary things with very little, coaxed flavour from the humblest materials, wasted nothing. I ate well in that poor place, better, in truth, than in richer ones, and the food told me a hard and admirable story: that this was a region that had learned, over long necessity, the deep art of making enough out of not quite enough.

subtopic: the food of a place and what it reveals
sentence: The first meal in a new country is a kind of greeting, and I take it seriously, choosing not the safe thing but the local thing, the dish the place is known by, and eating it carefully, attentively, as one might listen to a first sentence. This country's first sentence to me was a bowl of soup, sour and hot and complicated, and it told me at once that this would be a place of strong opinions and long traditions, and the rest of the trip, in flavour after flavour, bore the soup out.

subtopic: the food of a place and what it reveals
sentence: I learned to eat what the truck drivers ate, and the field workers, and the market porters, because the food of the people who work hardest is the food a place has perfected, the cheap sustaining delicious things, and following that rule led me, again and again, to the best meals and the truest rooms. The fancy restaurants performed a country. The workers' canteens simply fed one, and in the feeding, without meaning to, revealed it.

subtopic: returning to a place after years
sentence: I went back to the town after fifteen years and it had, of course, not waited for me, and the café where I had been happy was a phone shop now, and the woman who had run it was, the new owner thought, dead, and the view I remembered was half-built-over. The town owed me nothing. I had only borrowed it, once, briefly, and the loan had long since been recalled, and I walked its changed streets mourning a place that, for everyone but me, had simply, healthily, gone on.

subtopic: returning to a place after years
sentence: Returning to the city after a decade, I found that it had grown up around my memories, that the small district I had known was now ringed by towers, the quiet harbour now busy, the cheap quarter now expensive, and I walked it feeling like a ghost revisiting a house, the rooms rearranged, the new tenants oblivious. The city had moved on. I had not, quite, and the gap between my memory and the place itself was the real, slightly painful, souvenir of going back.

subtopic: returning to a place after years
sentence: The village, when I returned to it, had barely changed, and that was its own kind of shock, the same houses, the same well, the same long view, and I half expected my younger self to come round the corner. The village had simply held still while I had aged, and standing in its unchanged square I felt, sharply, the years, all of them, the village a fixed point against which my own passage was suddenly, mercilessly, measurable.

subtopic: returning to a place after years
sentence: I had loved the place once and I went back to check whether the love had been the place or the time of life, and the answer, I found, was both, inseparably, and the place without that time of life was just a place, fine, pleasant, but not the place I had carried for years. The magic had not been in the streets. It had been in me, in the particular open hungry self I had been when I first walked them, and that self had not made the return trip.

subtopic: returning to a place after years
sentence: Going back, I found the people had aged exactly as much as I had, which I had somehow not expected, the boy now a man with children, the woman now grey, the old man now gone, and the reunion was warm and strange and shadowed by the arithmetic. We had all kept moving, in our separate places, and now here we were, comparing the distances, and the place that had once held us all young held us now, kindly, in our middle age.

subtopic: returning to a place after years
sentence: I returned to the city expecting to feel at home and felt instead like a tourist with unusually good directions, knowing the streets but no longer known by them, and the loneliness of that was specific and unforeseen. You cannot return to a place you have left; you can only visit the place that has replaced it. The city was glad enough to have me. But it had filled the space I once occupied, as a sea fills a footprint, and there was no longer a shape there that was mine.

subtopic: returning to a place after years
sentence: The thing I had come back for was still there, against all odds, the particular bench, the particular tree, the particular angle of the harbour, and I sat on the bench under the tree looking at the harbour and the years closed up like a fan, and I was, for a few held minutes, both selves at once, the one who first sat here and the one who had come back. The place had kept the bench for me. It was more than I had any right to ask, and I was grateful, and I wept a little, and then I went.

subtopic: returning to a place after years
sentence: I returned to find the place had become famous in my absence, discovered, crowded, its quiet square now full of cafés with menus in four languages, and I felt a possessive, unreasonable grief, as if the place had been mine and had been taken. It had never been mine. I had been an early visitor, that was all, and now I was a late one, and the place, popular and prospering, did not need my private memory of when it had been a secret.

subtopic: returning to a place after years
sentence: Some places you should not go back to, and I knew that, and I went back anyway, and the returning was a deliberate, clear-eyed act of letting go, a way of replacing the bright fixed memory with the duller moving truth. The place was smaller than I remembered and more ordinary, and that was the gift of the return: it set me free of an idealised version, handed me the real and lesser and final one, and let the memory, at last, become a memory, and rest.

subtopic: returning to a place after years
sentence: I went back to the place after many years and found, to my surprise, that it received me not as a stranger but almost as a returning relative, that the café owner's son remembered the stories his father had told of the foreigner who once stayed a month, and that I had, without knowing it, become a small part of the place's own memory. I had thought I was returning to collect a memory. I found, instead, that I had left one, and the place handed it back to me, kept and warm.

subtopic: roads, paths, and the act of moving itself
sentence: There is a particular happiness that belongs only to the act of moving, of being underway, of watching a country come toward you and go past, and I have chased that happiness across half the world and found it reliably in the same place: not at the destinations, but in the long humming hours of the road itself, the engine, the window, the steady conversion of distance into having-been-there. The road is not the means. The road, I have come to think, is the thing.

subtopic: roads, paths, and the act of moving itself
sentence: The path went on ahead of me, climbing, dipping, curving out of sight, and the simple sight of it, the path itself, unwalked, promising, was enough to lift the heart, and I have felt that lift on a hundred paths in a dozen countries. A path is a kind of sentence the land has written, and to set off down it is to begin reading, and the not-yet-known of it, the next bend, the next rise, is the oldest and cleanest pleasure that travel has to give.

subtopic: roads, paths, and the act of moving itself
sentence: I love the moment of departure above almost any other, the moment the wheels begin to turn or the foot first lifts, the moment a place becomes a place I am leaving and the road becomes a road I am on, and the whole future of the journey is still ahead, intact, unspent. Nothing has gone wrong yet. Everything is still possible. The road stretches out clean and the heart goes quiet and glad, and I have set off, in my life, as often as I could, just to feel it.

subtopic: roads, paths, and the act of moving itself
sentence: The old road had been walked for so long that it had sunk below the level of the fields, worn down by the millennia of feet into a green holloway, a tunnel of trees, and walking it I was walking, literally, in the groove of everyone who had walked it before, the traders, the pilgrims, the soldiers, the ordinary people going about their ordinary lives. The road remembered them all in its very depth. I added my own light tread to the long worn total, and walked on.

subtopic: roads, paths, and the act of moving itself
sentence: The country road did not hurry and would not let you hurry, and so it taught a pace, the pace of looking, of noticing the hedge and the gate and the cloud, and I gave myself to that pace and the day grew longer and richer for it. We have built fast roads to defeat distance, and they do, but they defeat the country too, blur it, cancel it. The slow road keeps the country. The slow road, in fact, is the country, unrolling at the speed a person can actually receive it.

subtopic: roads, paths, and the act of moving itself
sentence: I have walked roads and ridden them and driven them and been carried down them on the water, and the means changes everything and changes nothing: the deep thing, the constant thing, is the motion itself, the being-in-transit, the particular suspended state of the traveller who has left one place and not yet arrived at the next. I am happiest in that state. The road is a kind of home to me, the only one, perhaps, that has never disappointed.

subtopic: roads, paths, and the act of moving itself
sentence: The track petered out into open hillside and I kept going anyway, off the path now, making my own way, and there was a particular thrill in that, in the moment a route runs out and the country itself becomes the route, and you navigate by slope and instinct and the look of the land. The path had been a kind of permission. Beyond its end I needed none. I walked the trackless hill in the wind, free of the road, which is its own and rarer pleasure.

subtopic: roads, paths, and the act of moving itself
sentence: The road climbed all afternoon and then, at the pass, simply tipped over and began, with relief, to descend, and the change was the whole drama of the day, the long effort and then the long reward, and I have felt that shape, that climb and crest and fall, on roads all over the world. A road has a narrative. It rises toward something and falls away from it. To travel a road well is to feel its story in the body, the strain and the cresting and the glad downhill run.

subtopic: roads, paths, and the act of moving itself
sentence: I have a weakness for the road that goes nowhere in particular, the minor road, the road the maps draw thin, because the major roads go to the major places and the minor roads go to the country itself, to the farm, the hamlet, the river, the long view, the actual texture of a land. I take the thin road whenever I can. It is slower and it is better, and it has shown me, over the years, a hundred places that had no name and needed none, and were enough.

subtopic: roads, paths, and the act of moving itself
sentence: At the end of the long day's road there is a tiredness that is also a kind of fullness, the body spent and the mind quiet and the country, all of it, the whole day's worth, settled somewhere inside, and I have lain down at the end of such days in rough beds in strange towns and felt richer than money has ever made me. The road takes the day and gives it back transformed, as distance, as memory, as the particular deep rest that only honest motion earns.

subtopic: crowds, fairs, and the press of people
sentence: The fair had drawn in the whole region, and the field was a churning sea of people and animals and stalls and noise, and I let the crowd take me, gave up steering, and was carried through the day on its currents, past the prize cattle and the cheap toys and the man selling something loudly from a box. There is a pleasure in surrendering to a crowd, in being, for a few hours, simply a drop in a great human flood, anonymous and warm and going wherever the flood goes.

subtopic: crowds, fairs, and the press of people
sentence: The pilgrimage crowd was the largest gathering I have ever stood in, a human mass that stretched beyond seeing in every direction, and instead of the panic I expected there came a strange peace, a sense of the individual self briefly dissolving into something vast and shared. The crowd had one purpose and I, for that day, borrowed it. We moved together, breathed together, an ocean of strangers made briefly one by a shared direction, and it was, unexpectedly, beautiful.

subtopic: crowds, fairs, and the press of people
sentence: The market on its busiest day was almost impassable, a slow hot crush of bodies through the narrow lanes, and you did not so much walk it as get digested by it, and yet the crowd had a courtesy, a give and take, a thousand strangers negotiating the same small space without malice. I let it carry me. It deposited me, eventually, breathless and grinning, out the far end, having shown me, in its press and heat and noise, the city at its most alive.

subtopic: crowds, fairs, and the press of people
sentence: The new year crowd filled the square to its edges and beyond, the whole city pouring in to see the year turn together, and I stood wedged among strangers in the cold, and when the moment came the crowd made one enormous sound, a roar of pure collective gladness, and I made it too. I had no one in that city. For that one shouted minute it did not matter. The crowd had taken me in, as crowds will, and let me belong, briefly, to everyone.

subtopic: crowds, fairs, and the press of people
sentence: The cattle fair was a fair the way fairs had been for centuries, before the word meant rides and candy, a serious gathering for the serious business of trading animals, and the crowd was a crowd of farmers, weathered, knowing, here to deal. I moved through it as an obvious outsider and was tolerated kindly. The fair did not perform for me. It went about its old loud business of beasts and bargains, and let me watch, and the watching was a privilege.

subtopic: crowds, fairs, and the press of people
sentence: There is a loneliness specific to standing still in a moving crowd, to being the one fixed point while the river of strangers parts and flows around you, all of them going somewhere, all of them belonging to the day in a way you do not, and I felt it once, sharply, in a festival crowd in a city far from home. It passed. Crowds give both things, the warm dissolving and the cold exclusion, and the traveller, sooner or later, in some crowd or other, feels each.

subtopic: crowds, fairs, and the press of people
sentence: The village fair was small, the whole crowd a few hundred people who all knew each other, and I, the one stranger, was conspicuous and, after the first hour, included, drawn into the games and the eating and the dancing by a community that had decided, collectively and without discussion, to absorb me. A small crowd cannot stay anonymous. It noticed me, considered me, and took me in, and I danced badly in a field with a village that, for one evening, lent me its belonging.

subtopic: crowds, fairs, and the press of people
sentence: The procession's crowd lined the route ten deep and waited, patient, good-humoured, for hours, and the waiting was itself the event, the crowd entertaining itself, the vendors working the queue, the children hoisted onto shoulders, and when the procession finally came the crowd rose to it as one. I had joined the wait early. By the time the spectacle arrived I had been so thoroughly folded into the crowd around me that its joy was, simply, mine.

subtopic: crowds, fairs, and the press of people
sentence: The fairground at night was a crowd lit by a thousand coloured bulbs, the noise enormous, the air thick with frying and diesel and sugar, and the press of people moved between the rides and the stalls in a slow happy churn, and I moved with it. The fair was loud and cheap and a little garish and entirely, infectiously joyful, and the crowd, all of it, every face, had come simply to be happy together, and was, and I, in its midst, was too.

subtopic: crowds, fairs, and the press of people
sentence: The harvest fair gathered the scattered farms of the whole high valley into one field, once a year, and the crowd was therefore a kind of reunion, neighbours who lived miles apart and saw each other rarely all crowding in at once, and the noise of it was the noise of a community briefly, gladly, assembled. I stood at the edge of all that gathering and felt the particular tender thing it was: a place too sparse to crowd, crowding, for one day, on purpose, for the joy of it.

subtopic: light, dusk, and the changing day
sentence: The light in that country was different, lower, more golden, slanting, and it changed the place utterly from the place the noon had shown me, gilding the plain stone, lengthening every shadow, and I learned to wait for it, to time my walking to the late afternoon when the country put on its best light and became, for an hour, unbearably beautiful. The midday country was merely a country. The evening country was a painting, and I walked into it, every evening, gratefully.

subtopic: light, dusk, and the changing day
sentence: Dusk was the hour the town came outside, when the heat let go and the light went soft and forgiving, and the streets that had been empty all afternoon filled with the slow pleasant traffic of the evening promenade. I joined it. The town walked itself, up the main street and down, greeting and pausing and being seen, and the dusk held it all in a gentle amber, and I understood that the town's true daily life began precisely when the sun began, at last, to go.

subtopic: light, dusk, and the changing day
sentence: The sunset over the water was a long slow performance, the sky cycling through its colours with an unhurried extravagance, and the whole waterfront had turned, without arrangement, to watch it, the strangers and the locals all facing the same way, briefly united by the simple wish to see the day out properly. The sun went. A collective small sigh. And the watchers turned back to their evenings, having attended, together, the day's quiet ceremonious end.

subtopic: light, dusk, and the changing day
sentence: First light in that valley was a slow blue thing, the dark thinning rather than breaking, the shapes of the hills emerging before their colours, and I made a habit of being awake for it, of stepping out into the cold half-dark to watch the country be assembled, piece by piece, by the strengthening light. The dawn was never the same twice. It was the one show the place put on free, every morning, for whoever cared to leave a warm bed and attend.

subtopic: light, dusk, and the changing day
sentence: The blue hour, the brief deep dusk after the sun is gone and before the dark is complete, was the loveliest time in the city, the buildings still visible but the lights now on, the sky a colour with no good name, and I learned to be out in it, walking, every evening, for those twenty minutes. The day-city and the night-city are two cities. The blue hour is the bridge between them, and to walk it is to be, for a little while, in both at once.

subtopic: light, dusk, and the changing day
sentence: The desert light at noon was a hammer and the desert light at dawn and dusk was a caress, and the whole rhythm of travel out there bent itself around that, the hard hours endured, the soft hours treasured, and I came to live for the long apricot light of the early evening, when the dunes glowed and the heat eased and the desert, briefly, was gentle. The same sun. The same sand. But the angle of the light remade the world, twice a day, completely.

subtopic: light, dusk, and the changing day
sentence: I watched the mountain change colour through the whole long evening, from grey to gold to a flushed rose to a deep blue and at last to a black silhouette against the stars, and I did almost nothing else for two hours, because the mountain, lit so, was enough, was a whole evening's worth of event. The light did all the work. The mountain merely stood there and let the departing day paint it, one colour after another, for anyone with the patience to watch.

subtopic: light, dusk, and the changing day
sentence: The fog burned off slowly through the morning, and the light came not all at once but in a long developing reveal, the sun a pale coin and then a brightness and then, at last, a clear command, and the country emerged from the white in stages, a tree, a hill, a far town, each one a small gift. I walked through the whole transition. By noon the day was ordinary and bright. But I had watched it being born, and that, somehow, kept it precious.

subtopic: light, dusk, and the changing day
sentence: The northern summer light did not properly end, and so the dusk went on for hours, a long luminous lingering, the sky a slow gradient that never quite resolved into night, and I found I could not go to bed, could not bear to, with the country still so softly, endlessly lit. I walked instead, for hours, through the long pale evening that would not become night, and felt the strange gift of a place where the day, generously, simply refused to be over.

subtopic: light, dusk, and the changing day
sentence: There is a particular light, ten minutes long, that comes just after sunset in clear weather, when the whole sky glows and the land below it is lit by no direct source but by the glowing sky itself, shadowless, even, gentle, and it is my favourite light in the world. I have stood still for it in many countries. It asks nothing and gives everything, this brief afterglow, this last soft exhalation of the day, and then it fades, and the stars come, and the travelling evening properly begins.

subtopic: why we go, and the question of travel itself
sentence: People ask me why I go, and I have never had a single answer, only a handful of partial ones: to see, to be changed, to feel the world's largeness, to escape my own small life and return to it altered. The truest answer is probably the simplest and the least respectable: that I am happy on the road in a way I have never managed to be anywhere else, and that this happiness, unaccountable and reliable, is reason enough, and has had to be.

subtopic: why we go, and the question of travel itself
sentence: I used to think travel was about the places, and I was young, and now I know it is mostly about the self, that we go abroad to come home different, that the real journey is the slow internal one the external one provokes. The places are the occasion. The change is the point. I have crossed continents to learn things about myself I could, in principle, have learned at home, but did not, and would not have, because home was too comfortable to make me look.

subtopic: why we go, and the question of travel itself
sentence: There is a kind of person who does not understand the wish to travel, who asks, reasonably, why leave a perfectly good home, and I have never been able to explain it to them, because the wish is not reasonable, it is older than reason, a restlessness, a hunger to see what is over the next hill simply because there is a next hill. I have it. I have always had it. And I have stopped apologising for it, and started, instead, simply obeying it.

subtopic: why we go, and the question of travel itself
sentence: I have wondered, on hard nights in cheap rooms, whether the travelling was a way of running from something, and I think, honestly, that it sometimes was, and that this is not the disgrace it is made out to be. We are allowed to need motion. We are allowed to find, in the road, a thing that the settled life withholds. The running, if that is what it was, also showed me the world, and the world, in return, slowly cured me of the need to run.

subtopic: why we go, and the question of travel itself
sentence: Travel does not make you wise, despite what is claimed for it; I have met fools who had been everywhere and sages who had been nowhere. But it does, if you let it, make you humble, by showing you, again and again, how many ways there are to live, to eat, to pray, to be happy, none of them yours, all of them sufficient. That is what I go for, in the end: not wisdom, but the humbling, which is rarer, and harder, and worth the fare.

subtopic: why we go, and the question of travel itself
sentence: The places blur, after enough years of going, the towns and the views running together, but the feeling does not blur, the particular feeling of being underway, of being a stranger in a place that owes you nothing and occasionally, astonishingly, gives you everything. That is what I am really collecting, I have come to see: not the destinations, but the recurrence of that feeling, and I will keep going, I expect, as long as the feeling keeps coming when I do.

subtopic: why we go, and the question of travel itself
sentence: I travel, I have decided, because it is the closest thing I have found to a cure for the great human disease of taking the world for granted, and the road, the genuine unfamiliar road, performs that cure reliably: it makes everything strange again, and strangeness is only another word for being properly, fully awake to a thing. I go to be woken. I come home awake. And then, slowly, home puts me back to sleep, and I have to go again.

subtopic: why we go, and the question of travel itself
sentence: The question is not really why we travel but why we come back, and the answer, I have learned, is that the coming back is part of the travelling, that a journey with no return is not a journey but an emigration, and that home is the fixed point that gives the wandering its shape and its meaning. I go out, and the world enlarges me, and I come back, and lay the enlargement down in the familiar rooms, and that double motion, out and back, is the whole of it.

subtopic: why we go, and the question of travel itself
sentence: I do not believe travel is necessary, or virtuous, or improving in any way it can be measured; it is simply a thing some of us are built to need, the way some are built to need the sea, or music, or solitude. I am built to need the road. I made my peace with that need long ago, and have spent my life, as far as I have been able, feeding it, and I do not regret a single mile, and I would, given the chance, go further.

subtopic: why we go, and the question of travel itself
sentence: In the end the reason I travel is the reason I have given last because it is the one that sounds least like a reason: that the world is very large and very strange and very beautiful, and that I have been given, by sheer luck, a brief turn at being alive in it, and that to spend that turn without going to look seemed, when I was young, an unbearable waste, and seems so still. So I go. I have always gone. And the going has been, by a wide margin, the best of my life.
